title: Italian Game (Giuoco Piano, slow c3/d3 plan)
summary: The easiest way for White to meet 1...e5. Quick development, castle, then a slow c3/d3 build-up before choosing between d3-d4 or a kingside attack with Nbd2-f1-g3.
ideas: Bc4 points at f7, Black's weakest square before castling.
c3 + d3 keeps the centre solid and prepares d4 later; it also gives the bishop a retreat (Bb3/Bc2).
Classic manoeuvre: Nbd2-f1-g3 (or e3) to bring a knight to the kingside.
h3 stops ...Bg4 and ...Ng4; a4 grabs space against ...b5.

article.whatIs: The Italian Game begins 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. White develops quickly, aims the bishop at f7 and gets ready to castle. This course teaches the calm version, the Giuoco Pianissimo ("very quiet game"), where White builds with c3 and d3 first and only then decides where to strike. It is a good way to learn how a classical opening works.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. If Black copies with 3...Bc5, continue 4.c3 Nf6 5.d3 for the Giuoco Pianissimo. After 3...Nf6 (the Two Knights Defence) the calm 4.d3 leads to the same kind of position.
pros: Very little forced theory: c3, d3, O-O, Re1 and Nbd2-f1 work against most Black set-ups.
Natural development: bishop to c4, knight to f3, castle early.
Flexible plans: you can later play d4, attack on the kingside with Nbd2-f1-g3, or gain space with a4 and h3.
Used by strong players as a low-risk way to keep the tension and out-manoeuvre the opponent.
You avoid the sharpest lines (Evans Gambit, Fried Liver) unless you decide to learn them.
cons: Black has solid ways to equalise, so White's edge is small and you have to win a long middlegame.
The slow build-up can feel aimless if you don't know the plans (the d4 break and the knight reroute).
Black can trade off the strong c4 bishop or free the position with ...d5.
It rarely gives a quick attack, so it suits patient players better than fans of fast tactics.

variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d3 d6 6.O-O a6 7.a4
variations.text: The core of the course. White keeps the centre solid and stops ...b5 with a4. Typical next steps are Re1, h3 and Nbd2-f1, followed by d4 or a kingside attack.

variations.name: Black breaks with ...d5
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5 4.c3 Nf6 5.d3 O-O 6.O-O d5 7.exd5 Nxd5 8.Re1
variations.text: Black frees the position at once. After the exchange on d5, Re1 puts pressure on e5 and keeps the game balanced but playable for White.

variations.name: Two Knights Defence with 4.d3
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d3 Be7 5.O-O O-O 6.Re1 d6 7.c3
variations.text: Playing 4.d3 instead of 4.Ng5 avoids the sharp theory and heads for a Pianissimo-style structure.

variations.name: Hungarian Defence
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Be7 4.d4 d6 5.d5 Nb8 6.Bd3
variations.text: A passive reply. White grabs space with d4-d5, pushes the knight back and keeps a comfortable edge.

article.againstIt: The most reliable way for Black to meet the slow Italian is to castle and play ...d5 at the right moment, trading pieces and reaching equality. Others chase the c4 bishop with ...Na5 or ...b5, or aim for ...Bg4 and ...Nd4 ideas. As White, don't drift: keep your pieces coordinated and strike with d4 when it is ready.

plans.white: Develop, castle, play c3 and d3, put the rook on e1 and meet ...a6 with Bb3 or a4. Then pick a plan: break with d4, reroute Nbd2-f1-g3 for a kingside attack, or expand with a4 and h3. There is no hurry because the structure is solid.
plans.black: Mirror the set-up with ...Bc5, ...d6 and ...O-O, tuck the bishop away on a7 when needed, and prepare the freeing ...d5. ...Re8, ...Nf8-g6 and ...Be6 are typical regrouping ideas.

article.history: The Italian Game is one of the oldest recorded openings. Players of the 16th and 17th centuries, including Gioachino Greco, analysed Bc4 ideas, and the names Giuoco Piano ("quiet game") and Giuoco Pianissimo ("very quiet game") come from Italian. After a long spell in which sharper gambits and the Ruy Lopez were more fashionable, the slow Italian has made a strong comeback at all levels, including top-level play.

faq.q: Is the Italian Game good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. The ideas are easy to understand (develop, castle, fight for the centre) and the slow c3/d3 set-up needs far less memorisation than the Ruy Lopez or the Sicilian. It teaches good habits.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Italian Game?
faq.a: Solid answers are 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) followed by ...Nf6, ...d6 and ...O-O, or 3...Nf6 (Two Knights). Black usually aims for the freeing move ...d5 once the king is safe.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Giuoco Piano and the Giuoco Pianissimo?
faq.a: Giuoco Piano is the whole opening 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Bc5. The Pianissimo is the quiet way White continues it: c3, d3, O-O, Re1 and slow manoeuvring instead of an early d4.

faq.q: Is the Italian Game still played by grandmasters?
faq.a: Yes. The slow Italian is a regular choice at the highest level because it keeps lots of play on the board with little risk.

title: Italian: the aggressive 4.Ng5 vs the Two Knights
summary: If you'd rather attack f7 straight away: 4.Ng5 against 3...Nf6. Includes the Fried Liver and the main line with 5...Na5.
ideas: 4.Ng5 + Bc4 doubles up on f7.
After 5...Na5 White keeps the extra pawn but must handle Black's lead in development.

article.whatIs: After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6, the move 4.Ng5 attacks f7 a second time and forces Black to react immediately. The best reply is 4...d5 5.exd5, after which Black either calmly gives the pawn back with 5...Na5 or walks into the Fried Liver Attack with 5...Nxd5?!. It is a sharp, tactical way to meet the Two Knights Defence.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5. Black's main reply is 4...d5, and you capture 5.exd5.
pros: Instant pressure: Black has to find accurate moves from move four.
Natural-looking replies such as 5...Nxd5?! can lead to a very dangerous attack for White.
The tactics are easy to remember, which makes it very effective at club level.
It teaches typical attacking themes: a double attack on f7, a king dragged into the centre, a pinned knight on d5.
In the main line 5...Na5 White wins a pawn that Black has to fight to regain.
cons: After 5...Na5 Black gets fast development in return for the pawn, and White must play carefully to keep the extra pawn.
Black can avoid it entirely with 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano), so you also need a second plan like the slow Italian course.
The main line needs accurate follow-ups (Bb5+, Be2, answering ...e4 with Ne5).
Well-prepared opponents can equalise, and the Traxler 4...Bc5 leads to wild play.

variations.name: Main line with 5...Na5
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 Na5 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 8.Be2 h6 9.Nf3 e4 10.Ne5
variations.text: Black's best and most common reply. The knight on a5 attacks the bishop, but White gives it a good retreat on e2 and keeps the extra pawn.

variations.name: Fried Liver Attack
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 Nxd5 6.Nxf7 Kxf7 7.Qf3+ Ke6 8.Nc3
variations.text: If Black takes on d5 with the knight, White sacrifices a piece on f7. The king is dragged to e6 and White piles up on the pinned knight. Strong defenders can survive, but it is very hard in practice.

variations.name: Traxler counter-attack
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 6.Bd5
variations.text: Black ignores the threat and counter-attacks f2. The safe practical reply is 5.Bxf7+, after which the king is stuck in the centre. 5.Nxf7 is much more complicated.

article.againstIt: Strong Black players answer 5.exd5 with 5...Na5, accept being a pawn down for a while and aim for quick development with ...c6, ...h6 and ...e4. Others avoid the whole line with 3...Bc5 or try the Traxler. The sharpest tries rely on White knowing the details.

plans.white: In the 5...Na5 line keep the extra pawn: retreat the bishop to e2, trade pieces when you can and meet ...e4 with Ne5. In the Fried Liver, bring the knight to c3, put the queen on f3 or e4 and keep attacking the exposed king and the pinned d5 knight.
plans.black: Give the pawn back only for development: ...Na5, ...c6 and ...h6 kick the white pieces, then ...e4 and ...Bd6 give you the initiative. Avoid 5...Nxd5 unless you know the defences.

article.history: The attack on f7 with 4.Ng5 has been known for centuries, and the Fried Liver Attack (also called the Fegatello) is one of the most famous beginner traps in chess. Modern analysis shows that 5...Na5 is Black's safest reply, which is why the Fried Liver mostly appears in games between inexperienced players.

faq.q: Is the Fried Liver Attack good?
faq.a: Against 5...Nxd5?! it gives White a strong, dangerous attack, and in practice most opponents struggle. Accurate defence can hold, so strong players usually avoid it with 5...Na5.

faq.q: What is the best response to 4.Ng5?
faq.a: 4...d5 5.exd5 Na5 is the main line, and it is considered the most reliable reply. The Traxler 4...Bc5 is the sharp alternative.

faq.q: Is 4.Ng5 better than 4.d3 against the Two Knights Defence?
faq.a: 4.Ng5 is sharper and gives more chances to win quickly, but also more risk and more theory. 4.d3 is the safer, quieter option.

faq.q: What is the Traxler counter-attack?
faq.a: It is the sharp reply 4...Bc5 to 4.Ng5, when Black lets White take f7 and counters on f2. White's safest answer is 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 6.Bd5.

title: London System
summary: One setup against almost everything: d4, Bf4, e3, Nf3, c3, Nbd2, Bd3. Low theory, solid, and easy to remember. The 2.Bf4 move order (before Nf3) is the modern choice.
ideas: Develop the dark-squared bishop to f4 BEFORE playing e3.
The pawn triangle c3-d4-e3 is very hard to break.
Keep h3 ready so the f4 bishop can retreat to h2 if Black plays ...Nh5.
Typical attack: Ne5, f4 and a kingside pawn storm, or Qc2 + Bd3 aiming at h7.

article.whatIs: The London System is a set-up for White that starts with 1.d4 and develops the dark-squared bishop to f4 before playing e3. White then plays Nf3, c3, Nbd2 and Bd3 against almost anything Black does. The pawn triangle c3-d4-e3 is very hard to break, and the opening is popular because it needs far less memorisation than the main lines.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4 and meet most replies with 2.Bf4, for example 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nf6 3.e3. Then add Nf3, c3, Nbd2 and Bd3. Putting the bishop out on move two keeps it outside the pawn chain.
pros: Very little theory: the same set-up works against 1...d5, 1...Nf6 and many other replies.
A solid pawn structure that is difficult for Black to attack.
Clear plans, such as Ne5 with f4, or Bd3 and Qe2/Qc2 aiming at h7.
Works well in blitz and online play, where you don't want to prepare for every opponent.
The f4 bishop is developed outside the pawn chain, so there is no "bad bishop" problem.
cons: Black can fight back with ...c5 and ...Qb6, hitting b2, and you must know the replies (Qb3, Qc1 or the Nc3 gambit).
If you play too passively, Black gets comfortable equality, for example with a mirrored ...Bf5.
It rarely gives White a real opening edge, so you have to outplay the opponent in the middlegame.
Well-prepared opponents find it predictable.

variations.text: When Black copies the bishop move, c4 and Qb3 put pressure on b7, which the bishop no longer protects.

article.againstIt: Players who know the London usually attack b2 with ...c5 and ...Qb6, hit d4 with ...Nc6, trade your bishop with ...Bd6, or play ...Bf5 and ...Nh5 to win the bishop pair. Meet each plan calmly: guard b2, keep h3 ready, and don't let your bishop get exchanged for free.

plans.white: Complete the triangle c3-d4-e3, play Nf3, Nbd2 and Bd3, then castle. After that choose between Ne5 with f4, Qe2/Qc2 and a kingside attack, or a central e4 break. Keep h3 handy against ...Nh5 or ...Ng4.
plans.black: Strike at the centre with ...c5 and ...Nc6, develop ...Bd6 to challenge the f4 bishop, and use ...Qb6 against b2 when it is safe. A Colle-style ...e6 and ...Bd6 set-up is also fine.

article.history: The system takes its name from the London 1922 tournament, where several players used it, although the ideas were known earlier. It stayed a favourite of club players for decades and returned in the 2010s and 2020s as a regular guest in elite and online play because of how little theory it needs.

faq.q: Is the London System good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. You play the same moves in most games, so you can concentrate on plans and tactics instead of memorising lines. It is one of the easiest openings to learn.

faq.q: What is the best response to the London System?
faq.a: Black's most testing set-up is ...d5, ...Nf6, ...c5, ...Nc6 and ...Bd6, hitting d4 and challenging the bishop. Early ...Qb6 and ...Bf5 plans also cause White problems.

faq.q: Is the London System bad?
faq.a: No. It is a sound opening that is used even by strong players. It just doesn't try to win an early advantage, so you need to play the middlegame well.

faq.q: What is the difference between the London and the Jobava London?
faq.a: The Jobava London puts the knight on c3 instead of d2 and often skips the quiet e3, aiming for a much sharper game. The classical London is calmer and more solid.

title: Queen's Gambit
summary: The classical 1.d4 2.c4. White offers a wing pawn to win the centre. Covers the QGD Exchange (Carlsbad), the QGA, the Slav, and the gambits Black can throw back.
ideas: In the Exchange QGD White's main plan is the minority attack: b4-b5 to give Black a weak c-pawn.
In the QGA White gets the pawn back easily. Don't try to keep b- and c-pawns.
Against the Slav, a4 stops ...b5 from holding on to c4.

article.whatIs: The Queen's Gambit starts 1.d4 d5 2.c4. White offers the c-pawn to deflect Black's d-pawn and take control of the centre. It isn't a real gambit, because White can win the pawn back if Black takes it. This course covers the Exchange Queen's Gambit Declined (the Carlsbad structure), the Queen's Gambit Accepted, the Slav and the gambits Black can try.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4 d5 2.c4. After 2...e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 the Exchange with 4.cxd5 exd5 5.Bg5 is a simple route to a clear plan.
pros: It fights for the centre without taking real risks.
Clear strategic plans, such as the minority attack in the Exchange.
A respected, well-tested opening that is played at every level.
It teaches pawn-structure thinking that transfers to many other openings.
White has easy ways to keep a small, lasting advantage.
cons: Black has many sound defences (QGD, Slav, Semi-Slav, QGA), so you need to know several systems.
The Exchange gives a symmetrical structure that can feel dry or drawish.
The minority attack is slow and requires patience.

variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3
variations.text: Black sacrifices a pawn for space. 4.Nf3 is the right move (4.e3? falls into the Lasker Trap), and a fianchetto gives White a pleasant edge.

variations.name: Chigorin Defence
variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.cxd5 Bxf3 5.gxf3 Qxd5 6.e3
variations.text: Black gives up the bishop pair for active pieces. White's two bishops and central pawns make up for the damaged structure.

article.againstIt: Black can take the pawn (QGA), support d5 solidly (QGD or Slav), or counter at once with the Albin Countergambit 2...e5 or the Chigorin 2...Nc6. The Semi-Slav (...c6 plus ...e6) is the most complex defence and is not covered here.

plans.white: In the Exchange QGD, play Bd3, Qc2 and Nf3, then the minority attack b4-b5 to create a weak c-pawn. In the QGA, regain the pawn with e3 and Bxc4 and take the centre. Against the Slav, use a4 to stop ...b5.
plans.black: In the Exchange, trade pieces and use ...Ne4, ...Bf5 or a kingside advance. In the QGA, play ...c5 and ...Nc6 to hit d4 and develop quickly. In the Slav, hold c4 with ...b5 only if it is safe.

article.history: The Queen's Gambit is one of the oldest known openings. It is mentioned in the Göttingen manuscript from around 1490 and has been played ever since by world champions from Steinitz and Lasker to Capablanca, Botvinnik, Karpov and Kasparov. The 2020 Netflix series The Queen's Gambit brought it fresh popularity.

faq.q: Is the Queen's Gambit a real gambit?
faq.a: Not really. If Black takes on c4, White can regain the pawn almost by force, usually with e3 and Bxc4, so it is more of a central fight than a sacrifice.

faq.q: Should Black accept the Queen's Gambit?
faq.a: Accepting with 2...dxc4 is sound, but Black must hand the centre to White in return. Many players prefer to decline with 2...e6 or 2...c6.

faq.q: Is the Queen's Gambit good for beginners?
faq.a: It is a great opening to learn because the ideas are classical and clear, but there are several defences to prepare for. Starting with the Exchange line keeps it simple.

faq.q: What are the main defences to the Queen's Gambit?
faq.a: The Queen's Gambit Declined (2...e6), the Slav (2...c6), the Queen's Gambit Accepted (2...dxc4), and the Albin and Chigorin countergambits.

faq.q: What is the minority attack?
faq.a: It is the plan of pushing White's b-pawn (b4-b5) against Black's larger group of queenside pawns, to create a weak pawn on c6. It is the key idea of the Exchange Queen's Gambit.

title: Ruy Lopez (Spanish)
summary: The most respected answer to 1...e5. White pressures the e5 pawn through its defender on c6. Covers the Closed main line, the Marshall, the Open, the Berlin (avoided with 4.d3), and Black's sidelines.
ideas: 3.Bb5 doesn't threaten e5 yet: 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.Nxe5 Qd4 gets the pawn back. It's long-term pressure.
The classic setup: O-O, Re1, c3, h3, d4 and the knight route Nbd2-f1-g3.
The Ba4-b3-c2 bishop can come back to aim at Black's king.

article.whatIs: The Ruy Lopez, or Spanish Game, starts 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. White attacks the knight that defends e5 and builds long-term pressure on Black's centre. It is the most respected reply to 1...e5, with a very deep theory and a rich variety of plans.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. After 3...a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O you have reached the main line.
pros: It fights directly for e5 and the centre, with long-term pressure.
Rich strategic play with many plans and a small but lasting edge.
Lines are heavily studied, so there is a lot of learning material.
The ideas you learn (the c3-d4 centre, manoeuvring knights) apply to many other openings.
Most of the elite players of the past 150 years have used it.
cons: A large amount of theory, especially against the Marshall, Berlin and Open lines.
Black has several very solid defences, and the Berlin Wall leads to a drawish endgame if White allows it.
Closed middlegames can be slow and manoeuvring.
Not an easy first opening for beginners.

article.againstIt: Black's main weapons are the Berlin Defence (3...Nf6 with an endgame after 4.O-O Nxe4), the Marshall gambit after 8.c3, the Open Spanish with 5...Nxe4, and sidelines such as the Schliemann 3...f5. This course sidesteps the first two with 4.d3 and 8.a4.

plans.white: Keep the pressure on c6 and e5, castle and play Re1, c3 and d4. The Nbd2-f1-g3 manoeuvre brings a knight to the kingside, and the bishop on c2 or b3 eyes the diagonal toward Black's king.
plans.black: Break in the centre with ...d5 or ...c5, use the ...Na5 and ...c5 plan in the Chigorin, or sacrifice a pawn for activity in the Marshall. The Berlin trades queens to reach a solid endgame.

article.history: The opening is named after the Spanish priest Ruy López de Segura, who discussed 3.Bb5 in his 1561 book on chess. Steinitz and Lasker made it a mainstay, and it has been played by almost every top player since, including Capablanca, Fischer, Karpov, Kasparov and Carlsen. The Berlin Defence became famous as a "Berlin Wall" after Kramnik used it against Kasparov in 2000.

faq.q: What is the Ruy Lopez?
faq.a: It is the opening 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5, where White attacks the defender of the e5 pawn. It is also called the Spanish Game and is one of the oldest and most respected openings.

faq.q: Is the Ruy Lopez good for beginners?
faq.a: It is a great opening to learn the ideas of strategy, but it has a lot of theory. Beginners may do better with the Italian Game first and move to the Ruy later.

faq.q: What is the Marshall Attack?
faq.a: It is a pawn sacrifice by Black (8...d5) after 8.c3, giving Black a strong attack. White can avoid it with the Anti-Marshall 8.a4 or 8.h3.

faq.q: How can White avoid the Berlin endgame?
faq.a: Play 4.d3 instead of 4.O-O. After 4...Bc5 5.c3 White keeps all the pieces on the board and a flexible position.

faq.q: Why is it called the Spanish Game?
faq.a: It is named after Ruy López, a Spanish priest who described it in 1561. In English-speaking countries it is called the Ruy Lopez, and in many other languages the Spanish Game.

title: Scotch Game
summary: Open the centre at once with 3.d4. More forcing than the Ruy, with less theory to memorise. A Kasparov favourite.
ideas: After 4.Nxd4 White has a free hand in the centre and quick development.
Against ...Nf6 lines, e5 kicks the knight and gains space.

article.whatIs: The Scotch Game begins 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4. White opens the centre immediately instead of building slow pressure like in the Ruy Lopez. After 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 White has a strong central knight, easy development and clear plans.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4.
pros: Open, active play with fast development.
Much less theory than the Ruy Lopez or the Italian main lines.
Clear piece play, so it is easy to understand what to do.
Used by world-class players to avoid the heavy Ruy Lopez theory.
White's knight on d4 is well placed and the centre stays under control.
cons: Black can reach equality with accurate play, for example 4...Nf6 or 4...Bc5.
There is less long-term pressure than in the Ruy Lopez.
You must know the answers to several different Black systems (4...Bc5, 4...Nf6, 4...Qh4).

variations.name: Classical 4...Bc5 5.Nxc6
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.Nxc6 Qf6 6.Qd2 dxc6 7.Nc3
variations.text: White trades the c6 knight and defends f2 with the queen. Black has the bishop pair, White has the better structure and a lead in activity.

variations.name: Classical 4...Bc5 5.Be3
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.Be3 Qf6 6.c3 Nge7 7.Bc4
variations.text: An alternative that keeps more tension: the knight is protected twice and White develops naturally.

variations.name: Mieses Variation 4...Nf6
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5 Qe7 7.Qe2 Nd5 8.c4 Ba6
variations.text: White kicks the knight with e5, then chases it again with c4. Black gets the bishop pair and active play but White has a space edge.

variations.name: Steinitz Variation 4...Qh4
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.Be2
variations.text: Black's queen comes out early. White develops with tempo and gives the e4 pawn back if needed to open lines.

article.againstIt: Black's most reliable moves are 4...Bc5 (hitting the knight and f2) and 4...Nf6 (pressing e4). The Scotch Gambit 3...exd4 4.Bc4 gives White another route but is not covered here. A flexible Black will try to trade pieces and use the bishop pair.

plans.white: Develop quickly, trade the knight on c6 when it helps (it damages Black's pawns), use e5 against ...Nf6 and aim for Qd2/Be3 or O-O-O ideas. Often White castles short and plays on the centre.
plans.black: Use the bishop pair with ...Bc5 and ...Qf6, hit e4 with ...Nf6, and look for ...d5 to free the position. In the Mieses, Black aims for ...Ba6 and ...Nb6 to harass White's pieces.

article.history: The opening is named after a famous 1824 correspondence match between the London and Edinburgh chess clubs, in which the Scots used 3.d4. It fell out of fashion after the 19th century, but Garry Kasparov brought it back at the highest level when he used it in his 1990 World Championship match against Karpov.

faq.q: Is the Scotch Game good?
faq.a: Yes. It is a sound opening that gives White easy development and open play. Black can equalise with best play, but the positions are rich and practical.

faq.q: Is the Scotch Game good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. The ideas are simple (open the centre, develop pieces quickly, castle) and there is much less theory to learn than in the Ruy Lopez.

faq.q: What is the Scotch Gambit?
faq.a: It is 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4, where White plays the bishop out instead of recapturing the pawn at once. It can lead to Italian-style positions or to sharp lines such as the Max Lange Attack.

faq.q: Why is it called the Scotch Game?
faq.a: It is named after the 1824 correspondence match between Edinburgh and London, in which the Edinburgh players used this opening.

title: 1.e4 vs Sicilian, Caro-Kann, French & more
summary: Completes a 1.e4 repertoire with low-theory, plan-based systems: the Alapin vs the Sicilian, Advance lines vs the Caro-Kann and French, and simple answers to the Scandinavian, Pirc and Alekhine.
ideas: Alapin (2.c3) builds a classical d4 centre without the Open Sicilian's mountains of theory.
The Advance (e5) systems gain space and give clear plans: c3, Nf3, Be2/Bd3.

article.whatIs: This course completes a 1.e4 repertoire with low-theory, plan-based systems against the replies other than 1...e5: the Alapin against the Sicilian, the Advance variations against the Caro-Kann and the French, and simple set-ups against the Scandinavian, the Pirc and the Alekhine. Every system is built around a plan rather than a long chain of memorised moves.
article.howToReach: Start with 1.e4 and choose the system by Black's first move: 1...c5 2.c3 (Alapin), 1...c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 (Advance), 1...e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 (Advance), 1...d5 2.exd5, 1...d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.Be3 (150 Attack), 1...Nf6 2.e5 Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.Nf3 (Modern Variation).
pros: One simple system per defence, so there is little to memorise.
All lines lead to understandable pawn structures.
Suits players who want to avoid the huge theory of the Open Sicilian or the Winawer.
The Advance structures give White space and clear kingside attacking plans.
The core ideas (c3 and d4, an e5 pawn chain) repeat across the different defences.
cons: White's advantage is usually small, so you must understand the plans to get anything.
Black has well-known antidotes (for example ...Qb6 and ...c4 in the French Advance, or ...d5 in the Alapin).
It isn't a complete repertoire, because it doesn't cover 1...e5.
Some systems can be passive if you don't follow the plan.

article.againstIt: Black's best chance is to strike at the base of the pawn chain: ...c5 against the French or Caro-Kann Advance, ...Qb6 to pressure b2 and d4, and ...d5 against the Alapin. Against the Pirc, ...c6 and ...b5 give counterplay, so avoid being too passive.

plans.white: Gain space with e5 or a solid c3 and d4 centre, develop the pieces naturally (Nf3, Be2 or Bd3, O-O) and then use your space for a kingside attack or a queenside expansion with b4.
plans.black: Attack the centre as early as possible (...c5, ...Qb6, ...Nc6) and don't let White enjoy a free space advantage. Bring the light-squared bishop out before locking it in with ...e6.

article.history: The Alapin Variation is named after Semyon Alapin (1856-1923), a Russian master who championed 2.c3 against the Sicilian in the late 19th century. The Advance variations of the French and Caro-Kann are also old ideas, and Aron Nimzowitsch did a lot to explain the strategy of the Advance French.

faq.q: What is the best way to play against the Sicilian Defence?
faq.a: The Open Sicilian (2.Nf3 followed by 3.d4) is the most ambitious choice, but it requires a lot of theory. The Alapin 2.c3 is a simpler option that still gives White a good centre.

faq.q: What is the Alapin Sicilian?
faq.a: It is the line 1.e4 c5 2.c3, preparing d4 so that a pawn can recapture. It is popular because it avoids the heaviest Sicilian theory.

faq.q: Is the Advance variation good against the French and Caro-Kann?
faq.a: Yes. It gains space and gives White clear plans, though Black has counterplay with ...c5 and ...Qb6, so you need to know the main ideas.

faq.q: Do I need to learn the Open Sicilian to play 1.e4?
faq.a: No. You can play Alapin, Grand Prix or other anti-Sicilians and still enjoy good positions. The Open Sicilian just has more theory.

title: Vienna Gambit
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4: an old-school attacking gambit. White builds a big centre, opens the f-file and castles early. Black has several good replies, so the course teaches the main ones plus the traps that punish natural-looking mistakes.
ideas: f4 fights for the centre and opens the f-file; if Black takes with ...exf4, White replies e5 or Nf3 and develops quickly.
The e4 pawn is not free: after 3...Nxe4? Nxe4 d5 the knight simply retreats and White is a piece up.
Against 3...d5 the plan is fxe5, Nf3, d4, Bd3 and O-O, keeping all the pieces working together.
Develop with tempo and keep your own king safe: the gambit is a fight for the initiative, not a blind attack.

article.whatIs: The Vienna Gambit goes 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4. By putting the knight on c3 first, White prepares f4 with the e4 pawn well protected. The aim is to open the f-file, grab the centre and attack quickly. It is a classic gambit that suits attacking players and rewards knowing the tactics.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 and, after 2...Nf6, 3.f4. If Black avoids 2...Nf6 you can still play f4 in many lines.
pros: Fast development and an open f-file give White an easy-to-understand initiative.
Many natural Black moves go wrong, such as 3...Nxe4? or the passive 4...Qe7.
The central pawn break d4 usually follows, and White's pieces are well coordinated.
Less theory than the King's Gambit and much safer for White.
A great surprise weapon at club level, because many players don't know the right answers.
cons: Against 3...d5 Black equalises with accurate play, so don't expect an advantage.
White sometimes gives up a pawn, so the compensation has to come from activity.
Black can avoid the main lines with 2...Nc6 or 3...Nc6 and aim for a quieter game.
You must be careful not to overextend: a careless attack can leave your own king exposed.

variations.name: Main line with 3...d5
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5.Nf3 Be7 6.d4 O-O 7.Bd3 f5 8.exf6 Bxf6 9.O-O
variations.text: The critical test. Both sides develop naturally and the position is equal, with chances for both. White's lead in activity is the main trump.

variations.name: Black takes: 3...exf4
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4 4.e5 Ng8 5.Nf3 d6 6.d4
variations.text: After 4.e5 the knight must retreat, and Black's best is 4...Ng8. White gets a big centre and an easy lead in development in return for the pawn.

variations.name: Greedy 3...Nxe4?
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 Nxe4 4.Nxe4 d5 5.Nf2
variations.text: A typical beginner's mistake. Black hopes to win the knight back with ...d5, but the knight has a safe square and White is a piece up.

variations.name: Flexible 3...Nc6
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 Nc6 4.fxe5 Nxe5 5.d4 Ng6 6.e5 Ng8 7.Nf3
variations.text: Black protects e5 and recaptures with the knight. White gains time by hitting the knight twice and gets a big centre.

article.againstIt: Players who know theory meet the Vienna Gambit with 3...d5, giving back the pawn and heading for an equal game. Others play the calm 3...Nc6 or take the pawn with 3...exf4 and retreat with 4...Ng8. The mistakes to avoid are 3...Nxe4? and 3...exf4 4.e5 Qe7?!.

plans.white: Develop quickly (Nf3, Bd3, O-O), take the centre with d4 and use the f-file. Don't hurry to attack: castle first and make sure your pieces are coordinated.
plans.black: Hit the centre with ...d5, develop the bishop to e7 and castle, and break with ...f5 or ...c5 when ready. Take the pawn only if you can return it at the right time.

article.history: The Vienna Game is named after the Austrian capital, where it was popular with players in the 19th century. The gambit 3.f4 is an old attacking idea that remains a surprise weapon at every level, because few players know all the details of the replies.

faq.q: Is the Vienna Gambit good?
faq.a: Yes. It is a sound opening that gives White easy development and a real initiative. With best play Black can equalise, but there are plenty of ways to go wrong.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Vienna Gambit?
faq.a: The most solid reply is 3...d5, hitting the centre at once. The calmer 3...Nc6 is also fine. Taking the pawn with 3...exf4 4.e5 Ng8 is playable but dangerous for Black.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Vienna Game and the Vienna Gambit?
faq.a: The Vienna Game is 1.e4 e5 2.Nc3. The Vienna Gambit is the sharp follow-up 3.f4, which offers a pawn. White can also play quieter ideas like 3.Bc4 or 3.g3.

faq.q: Is the Vienna Gambit good for beginners?
faq.a: It is a fun, tactical opening that teaches development, the centre and attacking play. It needs less memorisation than the King's Gambit, so it suits improving players well.

article.whatIs: The Danish Gambit begins 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3 dxc3 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.Bxb2. White sacrifices two pawns to bring the bishops to b2 and c4, where they bear down on Black's kingside. It is objectively risky, but it gives lively attacking chances and it is easy to play. Many natural replies lose quickly.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.c3. If Black takes with 3...dxc3 continue 4.Bc4 cxb2 5.Bxb2.
pros: Fast development: both bishops and the queen come out with tempo.
Black's g7 and f7 pawns become targets, and one careless move can lose material.

article.againstIt: The best way to meet the Danish is not to accept too much. Players decline with 3...d5 or 3...Nf6, or take the pawns and then give one back with ...d5 to catch up in development. The classic mistakes are leaving g7 undefended and getting the queen exposed on d8 or d5.

plans.white: Develop with tempo, aim the bishops at g7 and f7 and look for Bxf7+ or Bxg7. Don't try to keep the sacrificed material: your goal is activity and a safe king.
plans.black: Return a pawn at the right moment with ...d5, develop calmly with ...Nf6 and ...Bb4+, and keep the g7 pawn protected. Castle quickly and use the extra pawns in the endgame.

article.history: The Danish Gambit is an old attacking idea, known since the 19th century. Over the years it has been a favourite of attacking players, particularly in quick games, and it still appears as a surprise weapon.

faq.q: Is the Danish Gambit good?
faq.a: Not objectively: with best play Black can keep a small edge. But it is a practical weapon because the attack is easy to play and the natural-looking defences often go wrong.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Danish Gambit?
faq.a: Decline with 3...d5 or take the pawns and then return one with ...d5. Keep the g7 pawn safe and develop your pieces before grabbing more material.

faq.q: Is the Danish Gambit good for beginners?
faq.a: It's a fun opening that teaches development and attacking ideas, but you shouldn't expect to win by force. Learn the tactical points well and play it in quick games.

faq.q: What happens if Black takes everything?
faq.a: If Black takes all the pawns and plays 5...Nf6 6.Nc3 Bb4 7.Qb3, White's pieces are active but Black remains two pawns up. That's why the line works best against inexperienced opponents.

title: King's Gambit
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.f4: the most romantic opening in chess. White offers a pawn for the centre and an open f-file. The course teaches the Muzio Gambit and the Kieseritzky, plus sound replies to the modern 3...d5, the Classical 2...Bc5 and the Falkbeer, along with a famous mating trap.
ideas: f4 fights for the centre and opens the f-file. After ...exf4, Nf3 stops ...Qh4+ and prepares Bc4.
The bishop on c4 aims at f7. If Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 and ...f6, watch for Nxg5.

article.whatIs: The King's Gambit starts 1.e4 e5 2.f4. White offers the f-pawn to deflect Black's e-pawn, take control of the centre and open the f-file for the rook. It is one of the oldest and most romantic openings in chess, full of tactics and sacrifices. It is objectively a bit risky, but it is enormously fun and effective in practical play.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.f4. After 2...exf4 continue 3.Nf3, and after 3...g5 play 4.Bc4.
pros: Fast development and an open f-file give White an early initiative.
Fun, tactical and instructive: you learn a lot about attacking play.
Many Black replies lose quickly to tactics (4...f6? 5.Nxg5! and mate).
Surprising for opponents who prefer to play their usual defences.
Rich history and a lot of classic games to learn from.
cons: Objectively it's risky: with best play Black has at least equality and sometimes more.
Your own king is exposed, so a slip can be fatal.
There are many different defences (2...d5, 2...Bc5, 3...d5, 3...Nf6), and the theory is large.
Some lines (like the Muzio) require precise knowledge to remain playable.

variations.text: A more positional choice: White undermines the g5 pawn and then recovers a pawn with active play. The name honours Lionel Kieseritzky, who lost the famous Immortal Game to Anderssen.

article.againstIt: Strong players meet the King's Gambit with solid replies: 3...d5 (the modern defence), 2...Bc5 (declining), 3...Be7 or 3...d6 (Fischer's Defence). The trick is to give back the pawn at the right time and to castle safely. The Falkbeer 2...d5 is also a dangerous reply.

plans.white: Develop quickly (Nf3, Bc4, O-O, d4), open the f-file and aim at f7. If Black keeps the pawn, break with d4 or sacrifice a piece to open the king. If Black gives it back, play for a healthy centre.
plans.black: Stop the tricks first: play ...d5 early, or hold the pawn only if you can do so without weakening f7. Keep your king safe and counter-attack in the centre.

article.history: The King's Gambit is one of the oldest openings in chess and has been analysed since the 16th century. It produced the famous Immortal Game between Adolf Anderssen and Lionel Kieseritzky in London in 1851. It was the main weapon of the romantic era, and Boris Spassky revived it at the highest level in the 1960s, famously beating Bobby Fischer with it in 1960. Fischer later published an article called "A Bust to the King's Gambit".

faq.q: Is the King's Gambit good?
faq.a: It's a risky but playable opening. Engines prefer Black with best play, but in human games it can be very effective because Black has to find many accurate moves.

faq.q: What is the best response to the King's Gambit?
faq.a: The most solid replies are 3...d5 (the modern defence) or 2...Bc5. Taking the pawn and then returning it with ...d5 gives Black comfortable play.

faq.q: Is the King's Gambit good for beginners?
faq.a: It's excellent for learning tactics and attacking play, but your king is exposed and you need to be careful. Treat it as a way to train your tactical eye.

faq.q: What is the Muzio Gambit?
faq.a: It is the line 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.Bc4 g4 5.O-O, where White sacrifices a knight for a strong attack on the f-file. It's a classic, but it's risky if you don't know the details.

faq.q: Why was the King's Gambit so popular?
faq.a: In the 19th century, attacking chess was fashionable and players enjoyed bold sacrifices. Modern defensive technique has made it rarer at the top, but it's still an exciting weapon at club level.

title: Jobava London
summary: 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4: a sharper cousin of the London System. The knight goes to c3 early, so Nb5 and the bishop on f4 can hit c7 and Black must be careful in the opening.
ideas: Nc3 and Bf4 both target c7: after Nb5 the pawn on c7 is attacked twice.
Black's most natural-looking moves, such as ...Be7 in reply to c3, lose material to Nxc7+.
Against passive set-ups, play e3, Nf3, Bd3 and h4 to build a kingside attack.
Keep the bishop on f4 if you can; if Black trades it off, recapture with a plan.

article.whatIs: The Jobava London is a sharper version of the London System that starts 1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4. By putting the knight on c3 early, White threatens Nb5 and a double attack on c7. The result is a flexible, attacking set-up with a lot of traps for Black and very little theory.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4, and after 1...d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 continue 3.Bf4. Black has many options at this point, and the course covers the most common ones.
pros: Black must be careful about c7 from move three, which leads to many mistakes.
Flexible: you can adapt your plan (e3 and Nf3, or h4 and Qd2) depending on Black's set-up.
Much less theory than the main lines of the Queen's Gambit or King's Indian.
Great for players who like attacking chess.
Used by strong players to win games quickly.
cons: Black can equalise with solid play, such as ...e6, ...Na6 and ...Bd6.
Without e3 or c3, the d4 pawn can come under pressure.
The bishop on f4 can become a target for ...Nh5 or ...Bd6.
You must remember the main tactical points; a careless Nb5 can backfire.

article.againstIt: Black's safest set-up is ...e6 with ...Bb4+ and ...Ba5, or ...Na6, to keep c7 covered. Others trade the dark-squared bishops with ...Bd6, push ...c5 to hit d4, or mirror White with ...Bf5. The key is never to forget c7.

plans.white: Use Nb5 and Bf4 to put pressure on c7, then complete development with e3, Nf3 and Bd3. If Black plays solidly, consider h4-h5 and a kingside attack.
plans.black: Keep c7 defended (...Na6, ...Bd6 or ...Qd7), develop with ...e6 and ...Be7, and hit the centre with ...c5. Trade White's f4 bishop when possible.

article.history: The set-up is associated with the Georgian grandmaster Baadur Jobava, who used 2.Nc3 and 3.Bf4 against 1...d5 so successfully that it became known as the Jobava London or Jobava Attack. It brought the London System to a new generation of attacking players.

faq.q: What is the Jobava London?
faq.a: It's a version of the London System with an early Nc3 (1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bf4), aiming for a sharp, attacking game rather than the quiet London structures.

faq.q: Is the Jobava London good for beginners?
faq.a: It's a fun attacking opening, but it requires you to know the tactics around c7 and the threats on the queenside. If you like to attack, it's a good choice for improving players.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Jobava London?
faq.a: A solid reply is 3...e6 followed by ...Bb4+ and ...Ba5 (or 4...Na6) to cover c7. 3...c5 is also popular, hitting d4 right away.

faq.q: What is the difference between the London and the Jobava London?
faq.a: The classical London keeps the knight on d2 and builds the c3-d4-e3 triangle. The Jobava London puts the knight on c3 and keeps the c-pawn flexible, leading to tactical play.

title: English Opening (Fianchetto System)
summary: 1.c4: a flexible flank opening. This course uses a single, simple system against everything: Nc3, g3, Bg2, Nf3, O-O, d3, then Rb1 and b4. It's a calm, strategic choice with very clear plans.
ideas: c4 and Nc3 take control of d5; the bishop on g2 adds pressure to the centre.
Against 1...e5 you play a Sicilian with an extra tempo: the Reversed Sicilian.
The typical plan is O-O, d3, Rb1 and a queenside pawn advance with a3 and b4.
Be careful with the d5 knight trick: when Black plays ...Nxd5, the bishop on g2 and the knight on c3 attack it twice.

article.whatIs: The English Opening begins 1.c4. Instead of occupying the centre with pawns, White controls it from the flank. This course teaches a single, simple system against nearly everything: Nc3, g3, Bg2, Nf3, O-O and d3, followed by Rb1 and a queenside pawn push. It is calm, strategic and easy to learn.
article.howToReach: Play 1.c4. After 1...e5 continue 2.Nc3, and develop the kingside with g3, Bg2, Nf3 and O-O. Against 1...c5 or 1...Nf6 the plan is the same.
pros: One system for almost every reply: g3, Bg2, Nf3, O-O.
A flexible pawn structure that can transpose into many popular openings.
Against 1...e5 you get a Reversed Sicilian, with an extra tempo.
Clear plans: Rb1 and b4, or d4 at the right moment.
Used by world champions as a safe way to avoid heavy theory.
cons: White doesn't take the centre immediately, so Black has many options.
The advantage is small, so you need good middlegame technique.
Some Black set-ups can transpose to unfamiliar structures (Slav, KID, Queen's Gambit).
The play can be slow, and some players prefer a more direct attack.

article.againstIt: Black's main options are 1...e5 (the Reversed Sicilian), 1...c5 (symmetrical), 1...Nf6 and the Slav/Queen's Gambit set-ups with ...c6 and ...e6. A good plan for Black is to take space in the centre with ...d5 early. Be careful to answer 1...e6 or 1...c6 by choosing a reasonable transposition.

plans.white: Develop with Nc3, g3, Bg2, Nf3 and O-O. Then play d3, Rb1, a3 and b4 to gain queenside space, or break with d4 when you're ready. Keep the bishop on g2 active.
plans.black: Challenge the centre with ...d5 or ...e5, develop naturally and try to keep your pieces flexible. Avoid being too passive.

article.history: The opening is named after the English master Howard Staunton, who used 1.c4 in his 1843 match against Pierre Saint-Amant. It became a mainstream choice in the 20th century, championed by Mikhail Botvinnik, and it is still widely used by grandmasters, including Garry Kasparov and Magnus Carlsen.

faq.q: Is the English Opening good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes, as long as you follow a simple system. The ideas are strategic and easy to understand, and there is less memorisation than in the main lines of 1.e4.

faq.q: What is the best response to the English Opening?
faq.a: 1...e5 and 1...c5 are the most common replies. 1...Nf6 and 1...e6 are flexible, and the Slav-style 1...c6 is solid.

faq.q: What is the Reversed Sicilian?
faq.a: It is the position arising after 1.c4 e5, where White is effectively playing the Sicilian Defence with an extra move. White's plan is to expand on the queenside with a3 and b4.

faq.q: Does the English Opening give White an advantage?
faq.a: A small one, as with most openings. The advantage is more about having a comfortable position with clear plans than a decisive edge.

title: Ponziani Opening
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3: White prepares d4 to build a full pawn centre. It is an old, simple system with little theory and some neat traps (3...d5 4.Qa4! and the pinned knight), but objectively Black has several comfortable answers, so treat it as a practical weapon rather than an attempt to refute 1...e5.
ideas: 3.c3 prepares d4, so that White gets the ideal pawn centre; Black must react at once with ...d5, ...Nf6 or ...f5.
After 3...d5, 4.Qa4! pins the knight on c6 against the king; defending e5 with 4...Bd6? loses a piece to 5.exd5.
Against 3...Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 do not rush 5.d5 (5...Bc5! is awkward); 5.Bd3 keeps things equal and healthy.
Do not expect an opening edge: the aim is a comfortable position with a clear plan and few lines to learn.

article.whatIs: The Ponziani Opening is 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3. White prepares to play d4 and take the full centre, and it avoids the heavy theory of the Ruy Lopez and the Italian. It is simple and flexible, but it also gives Black time, so with best play Black equalises comfortably.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 and then 3.c3. If Black replies 3...Nf6, continue 4.d4. After 3...d5 use 4.Qa4, and after 3...f5 play 4.d4.
pros: Very little theory: c3 and d4 is the plan against nearly every reply.
A flexible pawn centre with a safe king and natural development.
Traps such as 3...d5 4.Qa4 Bd6? 5.exd5 catch careless opponents.
Keeps the game balanced and gives you the initiative in the centre.
It teaches the basics of the open centre: pawn tension, pins and piece activity.
cons: Objectively Black equalises or is slightly better with 3...d5 or 3...Nf6, so White has no advantage.
3.c3 takes away the c3 square from the knight, which makes development less natural.
Black can steer into Berlin-like or French-like positions where the extra tempo for Black is a real asset.
The pawn thrust d4-d5 can overextend White if Black plays accurately.

article.againstIt: The soundest answers are 3...Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 (trying to exploit the early d5 push), and 3...d5 4.Qa4 Bd7 5.exd5 Nd4. In both cases Black gets an equal game. Black should avoid 4...Bd6? or other moves that leave the c6 knight pinned.

plans.white: Build the centre with d4, develop with Bd3 or Bc4, and castle. Keep an eye on the pin on c6 when you play Qa4, and avoid pushing d5 too early, since it can leave pieces loose.
plans.black: Hit the centre immediately with ...d5 or ...Nf6, and recapture on d4 to get a free game. Be careful about the pin after Qa4, defend e5 with ...f6 or ...Bd7, and use the extra tempo for development.

article.history: The opening is named after Domenico Ponziani, an 18th-century Italian player and writer who analysed it. For a long time it was regarded as an inferior alternative to the Italian and Ruy Lopez because it gives Black time, and it is still not a top-level choice. It lives on as a straightforward system with few theoretical demands.

faq.q: Is the Ponziani Opening good?
faq.a: It is playable and healthy, but it does not give White an opening advantage. Black has several comfortable ways to equalise, so it is best used as a low-theory system.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Ponziani?
faq.a: 3...Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4 and 3...d5 4.Qa4 Bd7 are the most solid. Black must avoid 4...Bd6?, which loses a piece to the pin on c6.

faq.q: Why play 4.Qa4 against 3...d5?
faq.a: The queen pins the knight on c6 to the king along the diagonal and attacks the e5 pawn indirectly. Black has to play carefully, and 4...Bd7 or 4...f6 are the correct defences.

faq.q: Is the Ponziani better than the Italian?
faq.a: Not objectively: the Italian gives White more chances for an advantage. But the Ponziani needs less memorisation, which is why many club players enjoy it.

title: Bishop's Opening
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4: White develops the bishop first and keeps every option open. Against 2...Nf6 the calm 3.d3 gives a safe, flexible game, and Black's greedy 3...Nxe4? simply loses a piece. Against 2...Nc6 and 2...Bc5 White often transposes into quiet Italian-style set-ups.
ideas: 2.Bc4 eyes f7 at once, and the bishop sits where it can't be harassed by ...d6 and ...Nf6 without a fight.
3.d3 against 2...Nf6 is the safe move: it defends e4 and Black's 3...Nxe4? 4.dxe4 loses a piece.
Delay Nf3 so that you can choose between f4, Nc3 and d4 depending on Black's setup.
Many lines transpose to the Italian Game (Giuoco Pianissimo), so the plans you learn there apply here too.

article.whatIs: The Bishop's Opening starts 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4. White develops the bishop to its best diagonal and decides later how to place the knights and the f-pawn. It is flexible and has little forced theory, which makes it popular with players who want a healthy game without learning long lines.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4. Against 2...Nf6 continue 3.d3, against 2...Nc6 play 3.Nf3, and against 2...Bc5 play 3.Nf3 followed by c3.
pros: Very flexible: it can transpose into the Italian Game or become an independent system.
Black's most natural replies, 2...Nf6 3.d3 Nxe4?, lose material.
No long forced theory; mostly moves based on common sense (d3, Nf3, c3, O-O).
It avoids the sharpest lines of the Two Knights and the Evans Gambit unless you want them.
The move order gives you choices, so you can adapt to your opponent.
cons: White gets at most a tiny edge; Black has several equal systems.
A slow d3-plan can look passive against ...d5, which Black can play early.
Black can try 2...Nf6 3.d3 c6 4.Nf3 d5, reaching a comfortable Philidor-style structure.
You do not get the instant attack of the Danish or the Vienna gambits.

variations.text: White builds a classical centre. After the bishops are traded, the pawn on d5 gives White a comfortable game.

article.againstIt: The most solid replies are 2...Nf6 3.d3 c6 4.Nf3 d5, or 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Nf6 and 2...Bc5. Black must avoid 3...Nxe4? and play ...d5 or ...d6 at the right moment. If you play Black, aim for a Philidor-style or Italian-style setup and trade the bishop if needed.

plans.white: Develop with d3, Nf3, O-O and Re1, then decide: play c3 and d4, or push the f-pawn with f4 when the position allows. Keep an eye on a trade of your bishop and avoid weakening f2.
plans.black: Put a pawn on d5 or d6, develop the pieces naturally, and consider ...Bc5 or ...Be7 with ...O-O. Do not take on e4 without a clear reason, since the d-pawn recaptures.

article.history: The Bishop's Opening is one of the oldest ways of playing 1.e4 e5 and appears in some of the oldest chess books. It was popular in the 19th century and later often transposed to the Italian Game. Today it is mostly a flexible alternative used by players who like a low-theory system.

faq.q: Is the Bishop's Opening good?
faq.a: Yes, it is a sound and flexible opening. It does not give White a big advantage, but it keeps lots of options and avoids heavy theory.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Bishop's Opening and the Italian?
faq.a: In the Italian Game the knight goes to f3 first; in the Bishop's Opening the bishop comes out first. Many lines transpose, but the Bishop's Opening gives White extra choices.

faq.q: Why does 2...Nf6 3.d3 Nxe4 lose a piece?
faq.a: After 4.dxe4 White has won a knight for a pawn. The queen sortie 4...Qh4 does not help because White can defend with 5.Qe2.

faq.q: Is the Bishop's Opening good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. The ideas are simple (develop, castle, keep e4 safe), and the middlegame plans are easy to understand.

title: Smith-Morra Gambit
summary: 1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3: White sacrifices a pawn for quick development, open lines and an easy attack. Objectively the gambit is roughly equal to slightly dubious (engines see Black fine with best play), but Black has many ways to go wrong, and the declines 3...Nf6 and 3...d3 are easy to handle.
ideas: After 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 White has a lead in development: Bc4, Nf3, O-O, Qe2 and Rd1 put pieces on open lines against the Black king.
Aim at the d-file and the e5/f7 squares; Nd5 and e5 are the typical tactical breaks.
Decline wisely: 3...Nf6 4.e5! Nd5 5.cxd4 gets a free-flowing game, and 3...d3 4.Bxd3 gives a quick lead in development.
Be honest: if Black keeps accurate, defends calmly and trades pieces, White is simply a pawn down, so play for pressure, not tricks.

article.whatIs: The Smith-Morra Gambit starts 1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3. White offers a pawn, and after 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 White trades it for rapid development, open lines and chances against the king. It avoids the vast Sicilian theory and sets practical problems, though objectively Black can defend.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 c5 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3. If Black accepts with 3...dxc3, continue 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.Nf3 and follow with Bc4, O-O and Qe2. If Black declines, use the lines below.
pros: Avoids the huge main-line Sicilian theory: one move order for nearly all Black replies.
Fast development and open lines; natural plans with Bc4, O-O, Qe2 and Rd1.
Black has many ways to go wrong, such as 3...Nf6 4.e5 Ne4? 5.Qxd4.
Many Sicilian players have little experience against it, so the practical results are good.
Teaches how to play with an initiative and how to use open files.
cons: Objectively Black is fine with careful play, so you have to prove the compensation.
If Black consolidates with ...d6, ...e6 and ...Nf6, White has only a small initiative left.
Some declines (3...d5, 3...e6) give a normal position where the gambit is just a Sicilian without an extra pawn.
You must be willing to play without the pawn for a long time.

article.againstIt: Black's soundest reply is simply to accept with 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.Nf3 and then play ...d6 and ...e6 or ...a6, trade pieces and blunt the attack. Declining with 3...Nf6 4.e5 Nd5 or 3...d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 also works, but then White gets an easy game. The danger for Black is greed and passivity: ignoring development in the opening costs more than a pawn.

plans.white: Develop quickly: Nc3, Nf3, Bc4, O-O, Qe2 and Rd1, then aim for e5 or Nd5 at the right moment. Be happy to play for pressure and avoid committing pieces too early.
plans.black: Accept the pawn, develop the pieces naturally with ...Nc6, ...d6, ...e6 and ...Nf6, and trade the active white pieces. Close the lines near the king and stay a pawn up.

article.history: The gambit is named after Pierre Morra and Ben Smith, two players who championed 3.c3 in the 20th century. It has long been popular at club level because it avoids the heavy theory of the Open Sicilian. Strong players have also used it as a surprise weapon, though it is rarely seen in elite games.

faq.q: Is the Smith-Morra Gambit good?
faq.a: Objectively Black can hold with good defence, so it is not a way to refute the Sicilian. But the gambit is playable, avoids vast theory, and gives White plenty of practical chances.

faq.q: Should Black accept the Smith-Morra Gambit?
faq.a: Yes, accepting with 3...dxc3 4.Nxc3 Nc6 5.Nf3 and then ...d6 or ...e6 is the most solid. Careful defence and piece trades are the best antidote.

faq.q: How do I play against 3...Nf6?
faq.a: Play 4.e5, which forces the knight to move. After 4...Nd5 recapture on d4 with 5.cxd4; 4...Ne4? is a blunder because of 5.Qxd4.

faq.q: What if Black declines with 3...d3?
faq.a: Take the pawn with 4.Bxd3 and develop with Nf3, Qe2 and O-O. White has an easy lead in development, though Black is still safe.

title: Caro-Kann Defence
summary: Solid and reliable. Black supports ...d5 with ...c6 so the light-squared bishop can develop outside the pawn chain (unlike the French). Covers the Classical, Advance, Exchange, Panov, Two Knights and Fantasy.
ideas: Get the c8 bishop to f5 or g4 BEFORE playing ...e6.
In the Advance, strike at White's centre with ...c5 and ...Ne7-c6 or -f5.
Typical endgames favour Black's healthy structure.

article.whatIs: The Caro-Kann Defence starts 1.e4 c6 and follows with ...d5. By preparing the central strike with ...c6, Black supports the d5 pawn and keeps the c8 bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain before playing ...e6. It is solid and reliable, with a healthy pawn structure and good endgames.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5. Then 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Bf5 is the Classical Variation, 3.e5 Bf5 the Advance, and 3.exd5 cxd5 the Exchange.
pros: A solid pawn structure with no real weaknesses.
The c8 bishop gets out before ...e6, which solves the French Defence's main problem.
Clear plans in all the main lines, and the theory is manageable.
Very good endgames: Black's structure is healthy.
Fewer early tactics than in sharper defences, so it suits players who like to stay safe.
cons: It can feel passive, and White often has more space.
White has aggressive options, such as the Fantasy (3.f3), the Panov attack (4.c4) and the Advance with h4.
Black has fewer winning attempts, and some positions are drawish.
You must know a few traps (for example the smothered mate with Nd6#).

article.againstIt: White's typical tries are the Advance (3.e5), the Panov-Botvinnik Attack (4.c4), the Exchange, the Two Knights (2.Nf3 and 2.Nc3) and the Fantasy (3.f3). Aggressive players also try Bd3 and h4 ideas. Watch out for tricks like Qe2 followed by Nd6# in the 4...Nd7 line.

plans.white: Use your space in the Advance with Nf3, Be2 and c3, support the pawn on d4 and prepare a kingside attack. In the Panov, play for activity against the isolated queen's pawn. Against the Classical, go for h4-h5 to chase the bishop.
plans.black: Bring the light-squared bishop out first (...Bf5 or ...Bg4), then play ...e6, ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6. Against the Advance use ...c5 and ...Nc6; against the Exchange expand with ...Bg4 and a queenside minority attack.

article.history: The opening is named after the English player Horatio Caro and the Austrian Marcus Kann, who analysed it together in 1886. It later became a favourite of strong players such as Capablanca, Petrosian and Karpov, who valued its solidity and strategic depth.

faq.q: Is the Caro-Kann good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. It has clear plans, a solid structure and relatively little forced theory. It's a good choice if you want a safe, dependable reply to 1.e4.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Caro-Kann Advance?
faq.a: Play 3...Bf5 followed by ...e6, ...c5 and ...Ne7-c6 to attack the pawn chain. The Short System with Nf3, Be2 and Be3 is the most popular White choice.

faq.q: Is the Caro-Kann better than the French?
faq.a: They are similar in spirit, but the Caro-Kann lets the light-squared bishop develop freely, which is why many players find it easier to play. The French gives Black more counterplay but a worse bishop.

faq.q: Is the Caro-Kann drawish?
faq.a: It can lead to quiet positions, but White has sharp options such as the Fantasy and the Panov, and Black can play for a win with the right choices.

title: 1...e5 for Black (Open Games)
summary: A complete, classical answer to 1.e4 with 1...e5. Uses 3...Bc5 against the Italian (avoids 4.Ng5 and the Fried Liver), the Berlin against the Ruy Lopez, and principled answers to the Scotch, Vienna, King's Gambit and other tries.
ideas: Fight for the centre with pieces: ...Nc6, ...Nf6, ...Bc5.
The ...d5 break frees the position in many lines.
Know the early traps: Scholar's Mate, Fried Liver, King's Gambit queen check.

article.whatIs: 1...e5 meets 1.e4 by claiming the centre immediately. The result is an open game, with quick development, plenty of tactics and clear plans. This course gives a reliable reply to each of White's popular tries: the Italian Game, the Ruy Lopez (via the Berlin), the Scotch, the Vienna, the King's Gambit, the Centre Game and the Ponziani. It also shows how to stop Scholar's Mate.
article.howToReach: Answer 1.e4 with 1...e5. After 2.Nf3 Nc6 choose 3...Bc5 against the Italian Bc4 and 3...Nf6 (the Berlin) against the Ruy Lopez.
pros: It fights for the centre directly, in line with the opening principles.
Open positions teach you tactics and good piece play.
Classical, well-studied structures with plenty of resources for Black.
A wide choice of replies later on (Italian, Ruy Lopez, Scotch) so you can grow the repertoire.
Good practical chances against inexperienced opponents who fall for early traps.
cons: White has many choices, so you must prepare answers to Ruy Lopez, Italian, Scotch and several gambits.
The Berlin Defence can lead to queenless endgames that feel passive.
Open positions punish mistakes quickly.
Some White gambits (Evans, King's Gambit) require specific knowledge.

article.againstIt: White's main attempts are the Ruy Lopez, the Italian, the Scotch and the sharp gambits (Evans, King's Gambit, Vienna Gambit). Weaker players also try early queen moves like 2.Qh5. The best strategy is to develop your pieces, castle and answer each tactic calmly.

plans.white: Build a classical centre with d4 or c3 and d4, develop the minor pieces, castle and put the rooks on the e- and d-files. Against the Berlin, aim for a small endgame edge on the kingside.
plans.black: Develop quickly (...Nc6, ...Nf6, ...Bc5 or ...Be7), castle and prepare the freeing ...d5. In the Berlin, the bishop pair and the solid structure give Black good chances in the endgame.

article.history: Positions that begin 1.e4 e5 are traditionally called Open Games, and they were the main battleground of 19th-century chess. The Berlin Defence got its "wall" reputation in 2000, when Vladimir Kramnik used it to beat Garry Kasparov in their world championship match in London.

faq.q: Is 1...e5 a good reply to 1.e4?
faq.a: Yes. It is the most classical answer. Black gets a solid centre, quick development and a wide choice of plans.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Italian Game?
faq.a: 3...Bc5 (the Giuoco Piano) is a solid choice. After 4.c3 Nf6 5.d4 exd4 6.e5 d5 Black gets active play. Against the slow 5.d3, play ...d6, ...O-O and prepare ...d5.

faq.q: How do I stop Scholar's Mate?
faq.a: After 1.e4 e5 2.Qh5 defend with 2...Nc6, then answer 3.Bc4 with 3...g6 to hit the queen. Don't play ...Nf6 until f7 is safe.

faq.q: What is the Berlin Defence?
faq.a: It is 3...Nf6 against the Ruy Lopez. After 4.O-O Nxe4 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8, Black has a solid endgame. It is very hard for White to break down.

title: Sicilian Najdorf
summary: The most fighting answer to 1.e4, played by Fischer and Kasparov. 5...a6 is a flexible move that controls b5 and prepares ...e5 or ...e6. Includes the main 6th-move systems and the anti-Sicilians Black must know.
ideas: ...a6 stops Nb5 and Bb5 and prepares ...b5 queenside expansion.
The ...e5 structure gives up d5 control in exchange for space and active pieces.
Black's counterplay usually runs down the half-open c-file.

article.whatIs: The Najdorf Sicilian arises after 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 a6. The little move 5...a6 stops Nb5 and Bb5, prepares ...b5 and keeps Black's options open for ...e5 or ...e6. It is the most respected, most complex and most fighting line in the Sicilian.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 a6.
pros: Rich counterplay: Black fights for the initiative from the very start.
Very flexible: you can choose ...e5 or ...e6 depending on White's set-up.
A long tradition of success at the highest level, with a huge body of ideas to learn from.
Excellent winning chances for Black if White errs.
...a6 neutralises many White tries (Nb5, Bb5).
cons: Very heavy theory, especially against 6.Be3 (English Attack) and 6.Bg5.
White can attack Black's king with fast pawn storms; mistakes are punished quickly.
You also need an answer to anti-Sicilians such as the Alapin, Moscow, Smith-Morra and Grand Prix.
Not an easy opening for beginners.

variations.text: White aims at f7. Black answers with ...e6 and ...b5 and plays for queenside expansion.

article.againstIt: White can attack with the English Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O, g4), the Bg5 lines or the Bc4 sacrifices, or avoid the Najdorf with anti-Sicilians such as 2.c3 (Alapin), 3.Bb5+ (Moscow), 2.d4 (Smith-Morra) or 2.Nc3 (Grand Prix).

plans.white: Castle queenside and storm with g4-g5 and h4, or use the Bc4 lines to attack f7. In slower lines aim for a space advantage with Be2, O-O and f4.
plans.black: Counterattack on the queenside with ...b5, ...Bb7 and ...Nbd7-c5, or fight in the centre with ...e5. Keep the king safe, and look for ...d5 when it is possible.

article.history: The variation is named after Miguel Najdorf (1910-1997), the Polish-born Argentine grandmaster who developed and popularised it in the 1940s. Bobby Fischer made it his main weapon against 1.e4, and Garry Kasparov used it throughout his career.

faq.q: Is the Najdorf Sicilian good for beginners?
faq.a: It is rich and educational, but the theory is very heavy. Beginners may enjoy the tactics but are likely to struggle with all the memorisation. Intermediate and advanced players get more out of it.

faq.q: What is the best move against the Najdorf?
faq.a: At the top level, 6.Be3 (English Attack), 6.Bg5 and 6.Be2 are all popular. There is no single best move, and all can lead to a fight.

faq.q: Why does Black play 5...a6 in the Najdorf?
faq.a: It stops White's pieces from landing on b5, prepares the ...b5 advance and gives Black time for ...e5 or ...e6. It is a flexible waiting and preparing move.

faq.q: How do I avoid theory against anti-Sicilians?
faq.a: Learn one simple answer to each: Alapin 2.c3 Nf6, Moscow 3.Bb5+ Bd7, Smith-Morra 2.d4 cxd4 3.c3 dxc3 and Grand Prix 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4 g6.

title: French Defence
summary: ...e6 and ...d5 build a solid wall and counter-attack White's centre with ...c5 and ...f6. Uses the Rubinstein (...dxe4) against both 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2 to keep the theory light.
ideas: The French has a problem bishop on c8. Play ...b6/...Ba6 or ...Bd7-e8-h5 to activate it, or trade it.
Against e5 always hit the base of the chain with ...c5, then attack e5 with ...f6.

article.whatIs: The French Defence starts 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5. Black builds a solid pawn centre and fights back later with ...c5 and ...f6. The French has a reputation for being resilient, and the classic strategic issue is the c8 bishop, hemmed in behind the e6 pawn.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5. Meet 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2 with 3...dxe4, and 3.e5 with 3...c5.
pros: A solid, compact pawn structure that is hard to break down.
A clear counter-plan against White's centre: ...c5 and ...f6.
The Rubinstein 3...dxe4 gives a simple, low-theory way to answer both 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2.
Great winning chances if White gets careless.
The positions have recurring themes, so you quickly build a feel for them.
cons: The light-squared bishop on c8 can stay passive for a long time.
In the Advance Variation Black has less space and must break with ...c5 quickly.
The Exchange Variation can be dry and drawish.
You must know how to meet the King's Indian Attack and other sidelines.

variations.name: Advance Variation
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Qb6 6.a3 c4 7.Nbd2 Na5
variations.text: Black hits the base of the pawn chain on d4. After ...c4 the knight heads for b3 and Black gets queenside play.

variations.text: White sacrifices the d4 pawn for activity. Black must avoid the trap 7...Nxd4? and accept the pawn only after ...Bd7.

variations.name: Exchange Variation
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 exd5 4.Bd3 Bd6 5.Nf3 Ne7 6.O-O O-O 7.Re1 Bg4
variations.text: A symmetrical structure. The bad bishop is freed, so Black develops actively and equalises easily.

variations.name: Rubinstein vs 3.Nc3
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 Nd7 5.Nf3 Ngf6 6.Nxf6+ Nxf6 7.Bg5 h6 8.Bh4 c5
variations.text: Black gives up the centre in return for simple development and then breaks with ...c5.

variations.name: King's Indian Attack
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e6 2.d3 d5 3.Nd2 c5 4.Ngf3 Nc6 5.g3 Nf6 6.Bg2 Be7 7.O-O O-O
variations.text: White plays a slow set-up. Black takes space on the queenside and aims for counterplay with ...b5 or ...c4.

article.againstIt: White can gain space with the Advance (3.e5), simplify with the Exchange (3.exd5), use the King's Indian Attack, or play 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2. Attacking players like the Bd3 and Qg4 ideas against a weakened kingside.

plans.white: In the Advance, support the pawn chain with c3 and Nf3, then use your space to attack the kingside. In other lines, play on the e-file and look for a Bd3 and Qg4 attack against the black king.
plans.black: Hit the centre with ...c5 and ...f6, and free the bad bishop with ...b6/...Ba6, or ...Bd7 and ...Bb5. After ...c4, play for the b3 and e5 squares.

article.history: The French Defence is said to be named after a famous correspondence match played between the cities of London and Paris in 1834, in which Paris used 1...e6. Viktor Korchnoi made it a lifelong weapon, and the French has been a staple of top-level chess ever since. The Rubinstein Variation is named after Akiba Rubinstein.

faq.q: Is the French Defence good?
faq.a: Yes. It is a sound, strategic opening played by top players. It rewards patience and a good understanding of pawn structures.

faq.q: What is the best response to the French Advance?
faq.a: Attack the pawn chain at once: 3...c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Qb6. Black puts pressure on d4 and then gets queenside space with ...c4.

faq.q: How do I deal with the bad bishop in the French?
faq.a: Trade it off, or reroute it with ...b6 and ...Ba6, or play ...Bd7-b5. In the Exchange the bishop is free, so the problem goes away.

faq.q: What is the Rubinstein Variation of the French?
faq.a: It is 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 (or 3.Nd2 dxe4 4.Nxe4), when Black gives up the centre for easy development with ...Nd7 and ...Ngf6.

title: Scandinavian Defence
summary: 1...d5 forces the play from move one. White's choices are limited, so it's very low theory. Black gets a Caro-Kann-like structure with ...c6, ...Bf5 and ...e6.
ideas: After 3.Nc3 the queen goes to a5 (or d6), out of the way of tempo-gaining moves.
Develop the light bishop outside before ...e6 (same as the Caro-Kann).

article.whatIs: The Scandinavian Defence starts 1.e4 d5. Black challenges the e4 pawn immediately. After 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 the queen goes to a5 and Black aims for a Caro-Kann-like set-up with ...c6, ...Bf5 and ...e6. Because the early play is forced, the theory is small.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 (or 2...Nf6). After 3.Nc3 Qa5 you've reached the main line.
pros: Very little theory because White has few real options.
Black decides the character of the game right from move one.
A solid structure and an easy set-up to remember.
Surprising for opponents who are not prepared.
The queen is placed actively on a5, pinning the knight on c3.
cons: The queen comes out early and White gains tempi attacking it.
White gets a lead in development and a bit more space.
Few winning chances against a well-prepared opponent.
Some lines (Nf3/d4) require care to avoid being pushed around.

variations.name: Main line 3...Qa5
variations.pgn: 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nc3 Qa5 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 c6 6.Bc4 Bf5 7.Bd2 e6
variations.text: The queen on a5 pins the c3 knight. Black develops with ...Nf6, ...c6, ...Bf5 and ...e6, getting a solid position.

variations.name: 3.Nf3 and 3.d4
variations.pgn: 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.d4 Bg4 5.Be2 e6 6.O-O Nc6
variations.text: If White does not play Nc3 the queen is not harassed. Black develops quickly and pins the knight with ...Bg4.

variations.name: Advance 2.e5
variations.text: A French-style structure, but with the bishop already outside the pawn chain, which is a real improvement.

variations.name: 2.Nc3
variations.pgn: 1.e4 d5 2.Nc3 d4 3.Nce2 e5 4.Ng3 Be6
variations.text: Black gains space with ...d4 and builds a solid centre.

article.againstIt: White develops with tempo (Nc3, d4, Bc4, Bd2, Nf3) to chase the queen and then castles, aiming to use the lead in development. The most annoying tries are the Advance and quick Nc3 plus Bc4 set-ups.

plans.white: Develop with gain of time, build the centre with d4, put the bishop on c4 and Bd2, and castle. Then play for the open lines in the centre.
plans.black: Develop your pieces calmly: ...Nf6, ...c6, ...Bf5 and ...e6, castle and break with ...c5 or ...e5 at the right time. Keep the queen safe from tempo-gaining moves.

article.history: The Scandinavian is one of the oldest recorded replies to 1.e4: it appears in a book by the Spanish writer Luis Ramírez de Lucena in 1497. It is also known as the Centre Counter Defence. Players at every level, including grandmasters in rapid and blitz, have used it for its simplicity.

faq.q: Is the Scandinavian Defence good?
faq.a: Yes, it is sound and very easy to learn. It might give White a small edge in development, but Black reaches a solid structure.

faq.q: Is the Scandinavian good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes. The moves are easy to remember, the plans are clear, and there is little theory to learn.

faq.q: Which is better, 2...Qxd5 or 2...Nf6?
faq.a: 2...Qxd5 is the classical choice and the simplest. 2...Nf6 is a gambit-like line that needs more theory, but it avoids the early queen moves.

faq.q: How do I handle 3.Nc3 in the Scandinavian?
faq.a: Move the queen to a5 (or d6) and continue with ...Nf6, ...c6 and ...Bf5. The queen on a5 stays active and pins the knight.

title: Queen's Gambit Declined (for Black)
summary: The classical, rock-solid answer to 1.d4. ...d5 and ...e6 with ...Nf6 and ...Be7, the Tartakower system against 5.Bg5, and setups against the Exchange, the Catalan and the London.
ideas: Freeing breaks: ...c5 and ...dxc4 followed by ...e5.
The c8 bishop is the problem piece. The Tartakower (...b6/...Bb7) solves it.
Against the Exchange (Carlsbad), meet the minority attack with ...Ne4, ...Bf5 or kingside play.

article.whatIs: The Queen's Gambit Declined, for Black, starts 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6. Black supports the d5 pawn instead of taking on c4. It is one of the most solid and respected defences to 1.d4, with a firm pawn centre and ideas based on ...Be7, ...O-O and the freeing moves ...c5 or ...dxc4 followed by ...e5.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6. Against 4.Bg5 play 4...Be7; against 4.cxd5 recapture 4...exd5.
pros: Rock-solid, with a strong pawn centre.
Rich in strategic ideas, so you learn a lot about structures.
Used by almost every world champion at some point.
The Tartakower and other systems solve the problem of the c8 bishop.
Flexible, with many ways to reach a good position.
cons: The light-squared bishop on c8 is hemmed in and needs careful handling.
White's minority attack in the Exchange can be unpleasant.
White has several options (Exchange, Catalan, London), so you need a few set-ups.
Black has less space and must be patient.

variations.name: Exchange (Carlsbad structure)
variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.cxd5 exd5 5.Bg5 c6 6.e3 Be7 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.Qc2 O-O 9.Nf3 Re8 10.O-O Nf8
variations.text: Black plays ...c6 and ...Nf8-g6 or e6, using kingside space or ...Ne4 to counter the minority attack.

variations.name: Tartakower vs 4.Bg5
variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e3 O-O 6.Nf3 h6 7.Bh4 b6 8.cxd5 Nxd5 9.Bxe7 Qxe7 10.Nxd5 exd5 11.Rc1 Be6
variations.text: The Tartakower: after ...b6 the c8 bishop gets out, and exchanges ease Black's cramped position.

variations.name: Catalan with 6...dxc4
variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.c4 e6 4.g3 Be7 5.Bg2 O-O 6.O-O dxc4 7.Qc2 a6 8.Qxc4 b5 9.Qc2 Bb7
variations.text: Black takes the pawn and uses the free time to develop the queenside. The bishop on b7 will fight the g2 bishop.

variations.name: vs the London System
variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nf6 3.e3 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nd2 e6 6.Ngf3 Bd6 7.Bg3 O-O 8.Bd3 b6
variations.text: The most testing set-up: hit d4 with ...c5 and ...Nc6, and challenge the London bishop with ...Bd6.

article.againstIt: White can play the Exchange with the minority attack, the Catalan with a fianchetto, the pin 4.Bg5, or the London System. Aggressive players may try quick Bg5 and Qc2 or Bf4 ideas. A trap to know about for both sides is the Elephant Trap after 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5 6.Nxd5?.

plans.white: Exchange on d5 and attack with the minority plan (b4-b5), or build with Nf3, e3, Bd3 and O-O. In the Catalan use the long diagonal and the c4 pressure.
plans.black: Complete development with ...Be7, ...O-O and ...Nbd7, then free the position with ...c5 or ...dxc4 and ...e5. Solve the c8 bishop with ...b6 and ...Bb7 or ...c6 and ...Bf5.

article.history: The Carlsbad structure is named after the Karlsbad (Carlsbad) tournaments of the early 20th century, and the Tartakower Variation after Savielly Tartakower. The QGD has been a main weapon of players from Lasker and Capablanca through Karpov and Kasparov.

faq.q: Is the Queen's Gambit Declined good for Black?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the most reliable ways to meet 1.d4, and it has been used by almost every world champion.

faq.q: What is the Elephant Trap?
faq.a: It is 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5 6.Nxd5? Nxd5! 7.Bxd8 Bb4+ 8.Qd2 Bxd2+ 9.Kxd2 Kxd8, when Black wins a piece. The d5 pawn looks loose, but it is poisoned.

faq.q: How do I deal with the bad bishop in the QGD?
faq.a: Use the Tartakower with ...b6 and ...Bb7, or play ...c6 and ...Bf5/...Bg4 before closing the position with ...e6. In the Exchange, ...Bf5 is also a good plan.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Exchange Variation?
faq.a: Keep the position flexible, play ...c6, ...Bd6 or ...Be7, castle and meet the minority attack with ...Ne4 or counterplay on the kingside.
