title: King's Indian Defence
summary: A hypermodern counter-attacking defence. Black lets White build a big centre, then hits it with ...e5 (or ...c5) and often launches a kingside pawn storm with ...f5-f4-g5.
ideas: The g7 bishop is Black's best piece. Don't trade it lightly.
When White closes the centre with d5, Black attacks on the kingside (...f5) and White on the queenside (c5).

article.whatIs: The King's Indian Defence starts 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6. Black lets White build a big pawn centre and then attacks it, usually with ...e5 or ...c5. The fianchettoed bishop on g7 becomes a monster on the long diagonal, and Black often launches a kingside pawn storm with ...f5-f4 and ...g5.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6, then castle and break with ...e5.
pros: Dynamic and double-edged, with great winning chances for Black.
A clear plan: ...e5, ...Nc6 and ...f5 in the main lines.
The g7 bishop becomes a powerful attacking piece.
A long tradition of success at the highest level.
You can play it against 1.d4, 1.c4 and 1.Nf3.
cons: A large amount of theory, especially in the Classical and the Sämisch lines.
Black is often cramped and under attack on the queenside, so mistakes are costly.
You must know many different White set-ups (Four Pawns, Sämisch, Fianchetto, Averbakh).
Not suitable for beginners.

variations.pgn: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nf3 Bg7 4.g3 O-O 5.Bg2 d6 6.O-O Nbd7 7.Nc3 e5 8.e4 c6 9.h3 Qb6
variations.text: A calmer line. Black keeps flexible and pressures d4 with ...Qb6.

article.againstIt: White can build a big centre (Four Pawns), play solidly (Sämisch, Averbakh, Fianchetto) or launch a queenside attack with c5. Time is critical: in the closed lines the side that attacks first often wins.

plans.white: When the centre is closed with d5, play on the queenside with c5, b4 and Nb5. Keep the kingside safe and don't be too slow, because Black's attack will be fast.
plans.black: Attack the centre with ...e5 or ...c5. In the closed positions, push ...f5, ...f4 and ...g5 and use the g7 bishop. In the Averbakh and Sämisch, ...c5 is the freeing break.

article.history: The King's Indian was developed by Soviet masters in the 1940s, with Isaac Boleslavsky and David Bronstein among its pioneers. It was later made famous by Bobby Fischer and, above all, Garry Kasparov. The Mar del Plata Variation is named after the Argentine resort city, where strong tournaments in the 1950s saw these lines played extensively.

faq.q: Is the King's Indian Defence good?
faq.a: Yes. It is a strong and ambitious defence, but it takes a lot of study. If you like to attack and enjoy dynamic play, it's a good choice.

faq.q: Is the King's Indian good for beginners?
faq.a: Probably not. The theory is heavy and the positions are sharp and double-edged. A more solid opening usually suits beginners better.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Sämisch?
faq.a: Hit the centre quickly. The course uses ...O-O and ...c5 after 6.Be3, and ...e5 is the other main idea. The key is to strike before White consolidates with Qd2 and long castling.

faq.q: What is the Mar del Plata variation?
faq.a: It is the main line of the Classical King's Indian where White plays 8.d5 and 9.Ne1, and both sides attack on opposite wings.

title: Stafford Gambit
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6!?: a pawn sacrifice with a lot of venom. Objectively it is dubious (engines give White a clear edge with best play), but the natural-looking moves for White, such as Bg5 and Nc3-Bc4, run into mating tricks.
ideas: After ...Nc6 and ...dxc6 the c8 bishop and the queen are free, and ...Bc5 plus ...Ng4 create threats against f2.
Know the main traps: 6.Bg5? Nxe4! (7.Bxd8 Bxf2+ 8.Ke2 Bg4 is mate) and, after 5.Nc3, 6.Bc4? Ng4 followed by 7.O-O? Qh4!.
The h-pawn push ...h5 and the knight jump ...Ng4 are typical ways to put pressure on White's kingside.
Be honest with yourself: if White plays carefully (5.d3, 6.Be2, Nf3 and Qe1) Black is simply a pawn down.

article.whatIs: The Stafford Gambit arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6!?. Black sacrifices a pawn and, after 4.Nxc6 dxc6, plays for quick development with ...Bc5, ...h5 and ...Ng4. It is objectively dubious, but White's natural replies often run into traps, which is why it is very popular online.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nxe5 Nc6. If White takes the knight, recapture with 4...dxc6 and aim to develop with ...Bc5.
pros: Many natural White moves lose quickly (6.Bg5?, 7.O-O? and others).
Easy to learn: the plan is almost always ...Bc5, ...h5 and ...Ng4.
Effective in blitz and bullet because the traps work against hasty opponents.
Open lines for your pieces from the start.
A great way to practise tactics and attacking ideas.
cons: Objectively unsound: with correct play White keeps the extra pawn and a clear edge.
Strong opponents who know the theory can play 5.d3 and 6.Be2, and then you're simply a pawn down.
White can decline with 3.Nc3 (Four Knights) and avoid the gambit entirely.
If you rely on traps, you may neglect the basic principles of development.

article.againstIt: Well-prepared players meet the Stafford with 5.d3 and 6.Be2, or 5.e5, and just consolidate the extra pawn. Others avoid it entirely with 3.Nc3, the Four Knights or Three Knights. The important thing is not to fall for the traps.

plans.white: Take the knight on c6, play d3, Be2 and O-O, and avoid Bg5 and Bc4 until Black's threats are under control. Then trade off the dangerous bishop and use the extra pawn.
plans.black: Develop fast with ...Bc5, ...h5, ...Ng4 and ...Be6, and make threats every move. Look for ...Nxe4, ...Qh4 and ...Bxf2+ tricks, but don't overextend if White finds the right moves.

article.history: The Stafford Gambit is a relatively obscure old line that became a sensation when International Master Eric Rosen popularised it in online games and videos in recent years. Its reputation rests on traps rather than soundness, and it is now one of the most popular "fun" openings on the internet.

faq.q: Is the Stafford Gambit good?
faq.a: Not objectively. With best play White keeps a clear edge, but it is a great practical weapon: many natural-looking moves lose quickly, and the positions are easy to play.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Stafford Gambit?
faq.a: The simplest is to take the knight, play 5.d3 and 6.Be2, castle and trade off the dangerous knight and bishop. Avoid 6.Bg5 and 6.Bc4 traps.

faq.q: Is the Stafford Gambit good for beginners?
faq.a: It's a fun, easy opening for beginners to learn, and it teaches tactics. Just remember that strong opponents can neutralise it, so also work on solid play.

faq.q: What is the Stafford mate?
faq.a: It's the sequence 5.d3 Bc5 6.Bg5? Nxe4! 7.Bxd8 Bxf2+ 8.Ke2 Bg4#, where White takes the queen but gets checkmated.

title: Englund Gambit
summary: 1.d4 e5!?: a pawn sacrifice that is unsound against correct play, but famous for its traps. Learn it to spring the famous mating trap, to punish careless blocks, and to know when White has found the only good move.
ideas: After 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 the queen threatens Qb4+ and a fork on b2 and f4.
Careless replies lose quickly: 5.Nbd2? Qxf4 wins a bishop and 6.Bc3? Bb4! leads to mate on c1.
Be honest: if White plays 6.Nc3! (or avoids the traps with 3.Nc3 and 3.e4) Black is simply worse.
Use it for fun and surprise, not as your only defence to 1.d4.

article.whatIs: The Englund Gambit is 1.d4 e5!?. Black immediately sacrifices a pawn for quick development, typically with 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7. It is unsound against best play, but it has several nasty traps that make it popular in blitz and online games.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4 e5. After 2.dxe5 continue 2...Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7.
pros: Several traps, including the famous mating trap 6.Bc3? Bb4! and the Qxf4 trick.
The plan is easy to remember: ...Nc6, ...Qe7, ...Qb4+ and ...Qxb2.
Surprising for opponents who expect a normal 1.d4 game.
Black's queen and bishops get active quickly.
Good for practising tactics and for learning how to punish natural but careless moves.
cons: Objectively unsound: White can simply play a better move and keep the pawn.
Strong players can decline with 3.Nc3 or 3.e4 and stay fine.
The queen goes on an adventure, so one mistake can lose by force.
It doesn't suit slow, positional play, and you need a separate sound defence against 1.d4.

article.againstIt: The best way to meet the Englund is to avoid the traps and consolidate: 3.Nc3, 3.e4 or 3.Bf4 (without Nf3) all keep the pawn or just give it back harmlessly. If White plays 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2, then 6.Nc3! is strong. Never block with the knight or play Bc3.

plans.white: Keep the extra pawn: play 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Qd5 or 3.Nc3, and develop calmly. After 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3! is the only good move.
plans.black: Play ...Nc6, ...Qe7 and ...Qb4+, then take on b2 only if you've calculated the consequences. If White defends well, regain the e5 pawn and aim for an acceptable position.

article.history: The Englund Gambit is a fringe opening that goes by several names. Strong players rarely use it, but as a surprise weapon in blitz it has plenty of fans, thanks to its collection of quick traps.

faq.q: Is the Englund Gambit good?
faq.a: Not objectively. With best play White is simply a pawn up and has the better game. It is a practical weapon only because it contains traps that catch inexperienced players.

faq.q: What is the famous mating trap in the Englund Gambit?
faq.a: It's the line 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Bc3? Bb4! 7.Qd2?? Bxc3 8.Qxc3 Qc1#, where White falls into a back-rank mate.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Englund Gambit?
faq.a: Take the pawn, develop with 3.Nf3, and after 3...Qe7 4.Qd5 or 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Nc3! White stays a pawn up. 3.Nc3 and 3.e4 are also fine.

faq.q: Is the Englund Gambit good for beginners?
faq.a: It's a fun trap-filled opening, but it's not sound. Learn it for the tactics, but also build a solid defence against 1.d4.

title: Traxler Counterattack
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5!?: instead of defending f7, Black counterattacks f2. It is a wild gambit with many traps, and it is playable against the safe replies.
ideas: Ignore the threat to f7 and counterattack: after 5.Nxf7 Bxf2+ Black gets a strong initiative.
If White takes with the bishop (5.Bxf7+ Ke7) the king is safe enough in the centre, and ...Rf8 and ...d6 follow.
Quiet White replies (5.O-O, 5.d3, 5.Nc3) can be met by simple castling, so you don't need to sacrifice.
Know the trap 7.Nxh7? Nxh7, which simply loses a knight for a pawn.

article.whatIs: The Traxler Counterattack, also called the Wilkes-Barre Variation, arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.Ng5 Bc5. Instead of defending f7, Black counterattacks f2. It is a very sharp, double-edged line with spectacular tactics, and it is riskier than the usual defences.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 and, after 4.Ng5, play 4...Bc5.
pros: Spectacular tactics and a lot of traps, making it a great practical weapon.
Takes White out of familiar territory, because many players don't know how to respond to 4...Bc5.
If White plays quietly (5.O-O, 5.d3, 5.Nc3), Black can just castle and have a comfortable game.
The ideas (a counterattack on f2, the knight fork on e4) are fun and educational.
It is the most aggressive way to meet the Fried Liver set-up.
cons: In the critical lines White keeps an edge, so it is risky against prepared opponents.
The king often has to walk to e7, which may feel uncomfortable.
The lines are very sharp, and one inaccurate move can lose quickly.
White can avoid the most extreme lines by playing 4.d3 instead of 4.Ng5.

article.againstIt: The most testing tries are 5.Bxf7+ followed by Bb3 and d3 (keeping an extra pawn), and the wild 5.Nxf7. Careful players can also play 4.d3 instead of 4.Ng5, avoiding it altogether. The key is to know the tricks, and to recognise when the position calls for castling.

plans.white: Take on f7 with the bishop, retreat it to b3 and play d3 and Nf3, keeping the extra pawn and trying to exploit the exposed king. Be careful with greedy knight moves.
plans.black: Use the f-file, castle if possible, develop with ...d6, ...Qe8 and ...Bg4, and look for tactics like ...Nxe4 and ...Bxf2+. If White plays quietly, simply castle.

article.history: The Traxler Counterattack is named after Karel Traxler, a Czech priest and chess player who analysed the line at the end of the 19th century. In the United States it is known as the Wilkes-Barre Variation, after the Pennsylvania city where it was popular.

faq.q: Is the Traxler Counterattack good?
faq.a: It's very risky: with best play White keeps an edge in the sharp lines. But it's an excellent practical weapon, and it's safe if White plays quietly.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Traxler?
faq.a: 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 6.Bb3 is the most accurate. Taking the knight on f7 leads to wild play, and quiet moves like 5.O-O allow Black to castle.

faq.q: Why is the Traxler also called the Wilkes-Barre Variation?
faq.a: In the United States it is named after Wilkes-Barre, a city in Pennsylvania, where the variation became popular.

faq.q: Is the Traxler good for beginners?
faq.a: It's a fun attacking weapon but needs concrete knowledge. Beginners may enjoy it, though the sharp lines require good calculation.

title: Petrov Defence
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6: instead of defending e5, Black counterattacks e4. The Petrov (or Russian Game) is solid, symmetrical and respected at every level. Learn the key idea: kick the knight with ...d6 before taking on e4.
ideas: After 3.Nxe5, play 3...d6! first. 3...Nxe4? loses to Qe2 and Nc6+ if you play it carelessly.
Only after 4.Nf3 take the pawn with 4...Nxe4. Then build a solid centre with ...d5, ...Be7 and ...Nc6.
Know the early traps: 5.Qe2 Qe7 6.Qxe4?? Qxe4+ and the knight fork on c6.
Against 3.d4 and 3.Nc3, the best plans are different, so learn each set-up.

article.whatIs: The Petrov Defence, or Russian Game, starts 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6. Instead of defending the e5 pawn, Black counterattacks White's e4 pawn. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4, the position is symmetrical and solid. The Petrov is one of the most reliable defences against 1.e4, popular for its safety and simplicity.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6. After 3.Nxe5 play 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4. Never take on e4 at move three.
pros: Very solid, with a good reputation at the highest level.
Symmetrical structures where Black has no real weaknesses.
Lots of drawing potential against stronger players.
Clear plans: ...d5, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...Nc6.
Learning the key idea (kicking the knight before taking e4) is easy.
cons: Can lead to symmetrical, drawish positions, so winning chances for Black are limited.
White can play 3.Nc3 or 3.d4 and avoid the main theory.
A single move-order mistake (3...Nxe4?) loses a queen.
The main lines (5.d4 d5 6.Bd3) require precise knowledge of the typical plans for both sides.

article.againstIt: White's best chances come from the main line 5.d4, the 5.Nc3 line and the 3.Nc3 or 3.d4 sidelines. The Cochrane Gambit (4.Nxf7) and the 5.Qe2 trap are rare. The key is to stay solid, develop quickly and avoid the early queen trap.

plans.white: Build a space advantage with d4, Bd3 and c4, castle, and try to use the pin on the e-file. Aim for a small but lasting initiative.
plans.black: Play ...d5, ...Be7 and ...O-O, then challenge the centre with ...Nc6 and ...Bg4. Keep the structure solid and look for equality, then seek small winning chances.

article.history: The Petrov Defence is named after Alexander Petrov, a Russian master who analysed it in the first half of the 19th century, and it is also called the Russian Game. It has been a regular choice of elite players for decades, because it is so reliable.

faq.q: Is the Petrov Defence good?
faq.a: Yes. It is a very solid defence against 1.e4 and has been used by world champions. It rarely gets Black into trouble if you know the theory.

faq.q: Is the Petrov Defence drawish?
faq.a: It can be. Many games end in draws between strong players, but there are lines where Black can play for a win, and White has to avoid mistakes.

faq.q: Is the Petrov good for beginners?
faq.a: Yes, as long as you learn the key idea: kick the knight with ...d6 first. It is simple, solid and teaches good principles.

faq.q: What is the best response to the Petrov?
faq.a: The main line is 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3. White can also try 5.Nc3, 3.d4 or 3.Nc3. Each of these gives a small edge at best.

faq.q: What happens if Black plays 3...Nxe4?
faq.a: If White plays 4.Qe2, Black must find 4...Qe7. The natural 4...Nf6?? loses the queen to 5.Nc6+.

title: Rousseau Gambit
summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5!?: Black hits the centre at once and offers the e5 pawn for open lines. It is objectively dubious (engines give White a clear edge after 4.d3 or 4.d4), but the natural-looking replies 4.Nc3? and 4.Nxe5? lose material outright.
ideas: 3...f5 attacks e4 immediately; if White ignores it, ...fxe4 opens the f-file and gives Black the centre.
Know the two big traps: 4.Nc3? fxe4 5.Nxe4? d5! forks bishop and knight, and 4.Nxe5? Nxe5 5.d4? Nxc4 simply wins a piece.
Against the sound 4.d3 do not rush ...fxe4: develop with ...Nf6 first and keep the tension.
Be honest with yourself: if White declines the tricks and develops calmly, Black is the one fighting for equality.

article.whatIs: The Rousseau Gambit is the move 3...f5 after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4. Black attacks e4 straight away and is ready to give up the e5 pawn or the shelter in front of the king in return for open lines and quick counterplay. It is objectively dubious, but several natural White moves run into tactics.
article.howToReach: Play 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6. If White plays the Italian 3.Bc4, answer 3...f5. After 3.Bb5, 3.d4 or any other third move you are outside this course.
pros: Natural White replies such as 4.Nc3?, 4.Nxe5? and 4.Ng5? lose material at once.
Easy to learn: the plan is ...fxe4, ...Nf6, ...d5 or ...d6 and castle, with no long theory to memorise.
Opponents rarely know it, so you get a fight from move three.
The half-open f-file gives you play against f2 as soon as you have castled.
A good school for tactics around e4, f2 and the e1-h4 diagonal.
cons: Objectively unsound: after 4.d3 or 4.d4 White keeps a clear edge.
Moving the f-pawn weakens your king, and ideas like Ng5 and Qh5+ can become dangerous.
White can decline with a quiet 4.d3 and Black has no forced route to compensation.
Strong players who know the right moves leave you worse; the opening is a practical weapon, not a sound repertoire.

variations.name: The 4.Nc3 trap
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5 4.Nc3 fxe4 5.Nxe4 d5 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Nf6

variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5 4.d3 Nf6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.O-O Bxc3 7.bxc3 fxe4 8.dxe4 d6 9.a4 Na5

variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5 4.d4 exd4 5.e5 d5 6.exd6 Qxd6 7.O-O Bd7 8.Re1+ Be7
variations.text: White opens the centre. Black has developed pieces and a lead in space on the kingside, but the extra pawn and the e-file give White the better game.

variations.name: Taking on f5
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 f5 4.exf5 e4 5.Nd4 Nf6 6.Nxc6 dxc6 7.d3 Bxf5 8.Nc3 exd3
variations.text: The greedy 4.exf5 is not a mistake but it hands Black time: ...e4 kicks the knight and the position is roughly level.

article.againstIt: The simplest plan is 4.d3 followed by Nc3, O-O and a slow build-up, answering ...fxe4 with dxe4. 4.d4 is also strong: the centre opens and the extra pawn tells. Avoid the pawn-grabs and the natural 4.Nc3 and 4.Nxe5, and avoid 4.Ng5? Qxg5, which drops a knight.

plans.white: Play d3 (or d4), develop the pieces, castle and only then look at the centre. If Black takes on e4, recapture with a pawn so that you keep the better structure, and use Ng5 only when it is a real threat.
plans.black: Hit e4, develop with ...Nf6, ...Bb4 or ...Bc5 and ...d6, and castle. Keep pieces active, avoid early queen moves, and be ready to use the f-file and the pins on White's knight.

article.history: The gambit is named after a 19th-century player called Rousseau and appears in old gambit literature. It has never been part of top-level theory and survives mainly as a surprise weapon for club and online games. Its reputation rests on traps rather than on soundness.

faq.q: Is the Rousseau Gambit good?
faq.a: Not objectively. With best play White keeps a clear advantage, mostly because Black's king is weakened. As a practical weapon against players who do not know it, it can score well.

faq.q: How should White meet the Rousseau Gambit?
faq.a: Stay calm. 4.d3 and 4.d4 both give White the better game. Avoid 4.Nc3? fxe4 5.Nxe4? d5, and avoid 4.Nxe5? Nxe5 5.d4? Nxc4.

faq.q: What is the main trap in the Rousseau Gambit?
faq.a: After 4.Nc3 fxe4 5.Nxe4?, the move 5...d5 forks the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4. White cannot save both, and Black wins a piece.

faq.q: Should I take on e4 against 4.d3?
faq.a: No. 4.d3 fxe4?! 5.dxe4 Nf6 6.Ng5 gives White a strong initiative against f7. Develop with 4...Nf6 first and take on e4 later.

title: Albin Countergambit
summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5!?: Black answers the Queen's Gambit with a counter-punch, sacrificing a pawn for a cramping pawn on d4 and quick piece play. It is objectively dubious (White keeps a modest edge with accurate play), but the Lasker Trap wins a queen after the tempting 4.e3? and the main lines with 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3 are rich in counterplay.
ideas: After 3.dxe5 d4 the pawn on d4 cramps White's pieces; Black gets space and targets c3 and e3 with ...Bb4+ and ...Nge7.
Develop with ...Nc6, ...Nge7 and ...Ng6 to win back the e5 pawn, instead of the usual ...Nf6, which loses a tempo to e5-e6 ideas.
Lasker Trap: 4.e3? Bb4+ 5.Bd2 dxe3! 6.Bxb4? exf2+ 7.Ke2 fxg1=N+! wins the white queen; promote to a knight, not a queen.
Don't fear the pawn deficit: after ...Ngxe5 Black often regains it, and the d4 pawn is hard for White to remove.

article.whatIs: The Albin Countergambit arises after 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5!? 3.dxe5 d4. Black gives up a pawn for a space-gaining pawn on d4, a lead in activity and the chance to recapture e5 with the knights. It is objectively dubious, but the d4 pawn is hard to challenge and the opening is full of traps.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5. If White takes with 3.dxe5, push 3...d4. Against 3.e3 or 3.Nc3 you are out of the gambit lines, so keep a second reply ready.
pros: Black gets a cramping pawn on d4 and easy piece play.
The Lasker Trap is one of the best-known queen traps, and it still catches players.
The setup with ...Nc6, ...Nge7 and ...Ng6 is natural and easy to remember.
Many White players have little experience against it and may drift into a bad position.
A real gambit with long-term compensation, not just a trap.
cons: Objectively dubious: with correct play (4.Nf3 and 5.g3 or 5.a3) White keeps a small edge.
White can refuse the gambit with 3.e3 or 3.Nc3 and get a normal game.
The d4 pawn can become a target if Black loses the initiative.
You are a pawn down for a long time, so passive play is punished.

article.againstIt: The soundest approach is 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3 or 5.a3, followed by Bg2, castling and a slow plan against the d4 pawn. Don't walk into the Lasker Trap with 4.e3? Bb4+ 5.Bd2 dxe3 6.Bxb4?, and don't push the pawns on the queenside without a reason.

plans.white: Develop quickly, castle, and try to blockade or win the d4 pawn, for example with Nb3 or e3 at the right time. Meet ...Ngxe5 with Nxe5 and keep the extra pawn if you can.
plans.black: Develop the knights to c6, e7 and g6 to win back e5, keep the pawn on d4 supported, and use the bishop on b4 and g4 for pins. Seek counterplay with ...Bg4, ...Qd7 and queenside castling.

article.history: The Albin Countergambit is named after the Romanian-born master Adolf Albin, who took it up in the 1890s. The Lasker Trap carries the name of the future world champion Emanuel Lasker. Strong players have used the gambit as a surprise weapon, but today it is more often seen at club level.

faq.q: Is the Albin Countergambit good?
faq.a: It is objectively dubious: with best play White keeps a modest edge. But it is a rich, tactical opening with a long-term space advantage, and it scores well against opponents who do not know the key ideas.

faq.q: What is the Lasker Trap?
faq.a: After 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Bd2 dxe3 6.Bxb4?, the sequence 6...exf2+ 7.Ke2 fxg1=N+! 8.Rxg1 Bg4+ wins the white queen. White should play 6.fxe3 instead.

faq.q: Why promote to a knight in the Lasker Trap?
faq.a: A new queen on g1 would only trade queens with check and let White escape. The knight gives check and keeps the bishop on g4 ready to win the queen on d1.

faq.q: How should White decline the Albin?
faq.a: 3.e3 and 3.Nc3 are the quiet ways. After 3.dxe5 d4 White can play 4.Nf3 with 5.g3, or 5.a3, and keep a small edge.

title: Budapest Gambit
summary: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5!?: Black offers a pawn at once, aiming to win it back with ...Ng4 and ...Nxe5 and to get quick, active piece play. Objectively White keeps a small edge (about half a pawn) with accurate play, but the gambit is sound enough for serious use and hides the Kieninger Trap: 7.a3? Ngxe5 8.axb4?? Nd3#.
ideas: After 3.dxe5 Ng4 the pawn on e5 is hard to hold: ...Nc6, ...Bb4+ and ...Qe7 pile up on it, and Black almost always regains it.
Kieninger Trap: 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3? Ngxe5! 8.axb4?? Nd3# - a smothered mate with the king boxed in by its own pieces.
Against 4.Bf4 and 4.Nf3 the setup is the same: ...Nc6, ...Bb4+ and ...Qe7; against 4.e4 recapture on e5 with the other knight and develop.
Be honest: if White finds the best moves (the knight to d2, not c3, and the right pawn moves), Black is simply a little worse for a long time.

article.whatIs: The Budapest Gambit begins 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5, offering a pawn immediately. After 3.dxe5 Ng4 Black attacks e5 and plans to win it back, so the real price is some tempi and a slightly worse position. It is a respectable surprise weapon against d4 players, with an unusually popular quick win in the Kieninger Trap.
article.howToReach: Play 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5. If White takes with 3.dxe5, play 3...Ng4. If White declines with 3.e3 or 3.d5, you are out of the gambit and have to play a normal game.
pros: Fast piece play: the knight, bishop and queen all come to the centre with tempo.
A short, forcing opening with a clear plan, so there is little to memorise.
The Kieninger Trap (a mate in the opening) catches careless opponents.
Sound enough that Black rarely falls into a lost position by force.
A change from the main defences to 1.d4; good for players who want a sharp but real opening.
cons: Objectively White keeps a small but lasting advantage.
White can avoid the gambit with 3.d5 or 3.e3 (the latter is rare).
Black is a pawn down for a while if White finds the best defence, such as Bf4 followed by Nd2.
Some lines require precise play, and the early bishop check on b4 can lose time.

article.againstIt: The most reliable plan is 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3, then Nbd2 (not Nc3) and e3 or a3 to meet ...Bb4+ and ...Qe7. White must avoid taking the bishop on b4 at the wrong moment: 7.a3?? Ngxe5 8.axb4?? Nd3# is mate. 3.d5 and 3.e3 avoid the gambit altogether.

plans.white: Develop with Bf4, Nf3 and Nbd2, meet ...Bb4+ with Nbd2 and keep the king safe. Try to keep the extra pawn on e5, or give it back for a lasting edge in space and development.
plans.black: Win the pawn back with ...Nc6, ...Ng4xe5 and develop with ...Bb4+, ...Qe7 and ...d6. Castle quickly, trade pieces if you are fine, and look for tactics on the e-file and e1-h4 diagonal.

article.history: The gambit takes its name from the city of Budapest, where it appeared in master games in the 1890s. It had its heyday in the 1920s, when several strong masters tried it. Since then 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 has been seen as giving White a small edge, so the Budapest is mostly a surprise weapon. The Kieninger Trap is named after the master Georg Kieninger.

faq.q: Is the Budapest Gambit good?
faq.a: It is a respectable, sound surprise weapon rather than a refuted gimmick. White can keep a small advantage with accurate play, but Black gets easy development and real counterplay.

faq.q: What is the Kieninger Trap?
faq.a: After 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3? Ngxe5 8.axb4?? the knight jumps to d3 and it is checkmate, because the pinned e2 pawn and the king's own pieces leave no escape.

faq.q: How should White decline the Budapest?
faq.a: 3.d5 and 3.e3 are the main ways. The best is to accept the pawn with 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 and play Nf3 and Nbd2 with care.

faq.q: Why not play 3...Ne4 instead of 3...Ng4?
faq.a: The knight on e4 can be kicked with Nd2 or Qc2, but 3...Ng4 attacks e5 more directly and prepares ...Nc6 and ...Nxe5 in one move.

title: Opening Traps Every Player Should Know
summary: Short, memorable traps. Learn them to spring them, and more importantly, to avoid falling into them. Good for daily 'puzzle-style' reps.
ideas: Most traps punish greed (taking a poisoned pawn) or neglect (ignoring f7/f2).

article.whatIs: A collection of short, famous opening traps: Scholar's Mate, Fool's Mate, Légal's Mate, the Blackburne Shilling, the Englund and Budapest traps, the Elephant and Lasker traps, Noah's Ark, the Fried Liver and the Milner-Barry queen trap. Each line shows the tempting blunder and the punishment, so you can spot them from either side of the board.
article.howToReach: There is no single move order; each trap starts from a different opening, for example 1.e4 e5 (Légal, Blackburne, Scholar's), 1.d4 d5 2.c4 (Elephant, Lasker) or 1.e4 c6 (the Caro-Kann smothered mate).
pros: Quick, memorable puzzles that train your tactical eye.
You learn what not to do as well as how to win.
Many traps work at club level because players move too fast.
Each line is short, so it is perfect for daily practice.
The patterns (a smothered mate, a pinned knight, a fork) appear again and again in real games.
cons: Strong opponents won't fall for them, so you can't rely on traps alone.
Some traps only work against one specific mistake.
Traps aren't a full opening repertoire; you still need sound opening knowledge.

variations.name: Légal's Mate
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Bg4 4.Nc3 g6 5.Nxe5 Bxd1 6.Bxf7+ Ke7 7.Nd5#
variations.text: White sacrifices the queen: the pinned-looking knight on f3 is not really pinned. Three minor pieces deliver a mate.

variations.name: Blackburne Shilling Gambit
variations.pgn: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nd4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 5.Nxf7 Qxg2 6.Rf1 Qxe4+ 7.Be2 Nf3#
variations.text: If White grabs the e5 pawn, Black gets a decisive attack and a smothered mate. White should play 4.Nxd4 or 4.O-O instead.

variations.name: Englund Gambit Trap
variations.pgn: 1.d4 e5 2.dxe5 Nc6 3.Nf3 Qe7 4.Bf4 Qb4+ 5.Bd2 Qxb2 6.Bc3 Bb4 7.Qd2 Bxc3 8.Qxc3 Qc1#
variations.text: A natural-looking attack on the queen loses to a back-rank mate. White must avoid 6.Bc3 and 7.Qd2.

variations.name: Elephant Trap
variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5 6.Nxd5 Nxd5 7.Bxd8 Bb4+ 8.Qd2 Bxd2+ 9.Kxd2 Kxd8
variations.text: Taking the apparently loose pawn on d5 loses a piece: the pinned knight isn't really pinned and a check wins the queen back.

variations.name: Lasker Trap
variations.pgn: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Bd2 dxe3 6.Bxb4 exf2+ 7.Ke2 fxg1=N+
variations.text: In the Albin Countergambit, a rare underpromotion to a knight wins material after the careless 4.e3.

article.againstIt: Traps rely on greed (grabbing a poisoned pawn), haste (ignoring a threat to f7 or f2) or unfamiliarity with a pin. Before you take any 'free' pawn or piece, ask what the opponent's last move threatened.

plans.white: Develop calmly and check each capture: if a pawn or piece seems to hang for free, look for forks, pins, discovered attacks and back-rank checks before you take it.
plans.black: Prepare simple traps (Blackburne, Englund, Légal) but never play a move you wouldn't be happy to play if the opponent doesn't fall for the trick.

article.history: Légal's Mate is named after the French player Sire de Légal (1702-1792), who was Philidor's teacher and is said to have played it in a game around 1750. The Blackburne Shilling Gambit is named for the English master Joseph Henry Blackburne, who reportedly won shillings from unsuspecting amateurs with it. Fool's Mate is the shortest possible checkmate in chess.

faq.q: Are opening traps worth learning?
faq.a: Yes, as long as you also learn sound opening principles. Traps teach tactical patterns, and they work well in quick games against weaker opponents.

faq.q: What is the fastest checkmate in chess?
faq.a: Fool's Mate takes only two moves from each side: 1.f3 e5 2.g4 Qh4#. It only happens if White plays two very weak moves.

faq.q: What is the Scholar's Mate and how do I stop it?
faq.a: It is the four-move mate 1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6 3.Qh5 Nf6?? 4.Qxf7#. Defend f7, for example with ...g6 or ...Qe7, and develop your pieces.

faq.q: What is the Englund Gambit?
faq.a: It is the line 1.d4 e5, in which Black sacrifices a pawn for quick development. It is risky against good play but has several nasty traps for the unwary.
